items.stem: The cartoon most directly expresses which point of view about the change in German leadership in March 1890?

options.text: The young emperor was discarding the seasoned statesman who had long guided the German state
options.label: key
options.why: The title calls the departing man the pilot, the expert who steers a ship through hazards, while the crowned young man watches from the rail. This casts Bismarck's exit in March 1890 as Wilhelm II setting aside the guide of the German ship of state.

options.text: British observers welcomed the chancellor's exit as a victory for liberal parties in the German Reichstag
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the image is about Reichstag parties, and calling the man a pilot honors him. The cartoon does not celebrate his removal.

options.text: The departing chancellor was abandoning a German state he believed was doomed to socialist revolution
options.label: reversal
options.why: The title says the pilot is being dropped by the ship. He is not choosing to leave, and the cartoon says nothing about revolution.

options.text: The German Empire was about to split apart into the separate kingdoms that had existed before 1871
options.label: overstated
options.why: The ship stays whole and still has its ruler on board. The cartoon is about who steers it, not about the empire breaking up.

facts: Otto von Bismarck left office as German chancellor in March 1890 after clashing with Wilhelm II.
Wilhelm II became German emperor in 1888.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The title calls the departing figure the pilot, and the crowned young ruler watches from the rail as he goes down the ladder.
design.evidence_quote: Dropping the Pilot

items.stem: The cartoon's portrayal of the departing chancellor as the pilot who had steered the ship is best understood in the context of his earlier role in

options.text: building alliances after 1871 that kept France diplomatically isolated
options.label: key
options.why: After German unification, Bismarck built a system of alliances, including the Dual Alliance of 1879, the Triple Alliance of 1882, and treaties with Russia. Its purpose was to isolate France and keep the peace. This is why contemporaries saw him as the pilot of German policy.

options.text: leading the Frankfurt Parliament's liberal effort to unify the German states in 1848 and 1849
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Bismarck was a conservative who opposed the liberal Frankfurt Parliament. He later unified Germany through Prussian wars instead.

options.text: shaping the Congress of Vienna settlement that restored the conservative monarchies in 1815
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Vienna settlement of 1815 was mainly Metternich's work, from long before Bismarck's career.

options.text: founding the Zollverein customs union that tied the north German states together in 1834
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Zollverein began in 1834, decades before Bismarck came to power in 1862.

facts: Bismarck concluded the Dual Alliance with Austria-Hungary in 1879 and the Triple Alliance with Austria-Hungary and Italy in 1882.
Bismarck's diplomacy after 1871 aimed to keep France isolated.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The pilot image ties the departing figure to the steering of German policy, which students link to Bismarck's diplomatic system after 1871.
design.evidence_quote: Dropping the Pilot

items.stem: Which of the following developments in European diplomacy in the 1890s most directly followed from the change in leadership shown in the cartoon?

options.text: Germany let its 1887 treaty with Russia lapse, and Russia soon allied with France
options.label: key
options.why: Once Bismarck was gone, Wilhelm II's government chose not to renew the 1887 Reinsurance Treaty in 1890. Russia then formed an alliance with France, finalized in 1894. That ended the isolation of France that Bismarck had kept in place.

options.text: Germany returned Alsace and Lorraine to France in order to ease tensions along the Rhine
options.label: reversal
options.why: Germany kept Alsace-Lorraine until its defeat in the First World War. Losing the provinces in 1871 remained a lasting French grievance.

options.text: Germany signed a formal alliance with Britain to block Russian expansion in Central Asia
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: No Anglo-German alliance was formed. Britain eventually settled its differences with France in 1904 and with Russia in 1907.

options.text: Germany withdrew from the Triple Alliance and ended its long military partnership with Austria-Hungary
options.label: reversal
options.why: After 1890, Germany tied itself even more closely to Austria-Hungary. That partnership lasted through the First World War.

facts: Germany did not renew the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia in 1890.
France and Russia concluded an alliance in 1894.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The cartoon shows the young emperor dropping the chancellor in March 1890, the change that came just before the treaty with Russia lapsed.

items.stem: After 1890, the young ruler shown at the ship's rail became most closely associated with which policy that alarmed many in Britain?

options.text: building a large battle fleet as part of a bid for global power
options.label: key
options.why: Wilhelm II pursued Weltpolitik, a bid for world power status. It included the naval expansion begun with the Naval Laws of 1898, which set off an arms race with Britain.

options.text: introducing state health and accident insurance to undercut the appeal of the socialists
options.label: misattributed
options.why: State social insurance was Bismarck's program of the 1880s, introduced before Wilhelm II took the throne.

options.text: launching the Kulturkampf to reduce the power of the Catholic Church in German schools
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Kulturkampf was Bismarck's campaign of the 1870s, not a policy of Wilhelm II.

options.text: abolishing the elected Reichstag so that he could rule Germany as an absolute monarch
options.label: overstated
options.why: Wilhelm II asserted strong personal authority, but the Reichstag kept meeting throughout his reign.

facts: Wilhelm II pursued Weltpolitik, including German naval expansion under the Naval Laws beginning in 1898.
The German naval buildup contributed to Anglo-German rivalry before 1914.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The crowned young man in military dress at the rail is Wilhelm II, the figure the question is built on.

items.stem: Which of the following most limits the cartoon's usefulness as evidence of how Germans viewed the change in leadership in 1890?

options.text: It was made by a British artist for the readers of a British magazine
options.label: key
options.why: The credit line shows that John Tenniel drew the cartoon for the London magazine Punch. It reflects a British outlook and British readers, not German opinion.

options.text: It was drawn many years after the events it depicts and relies on uncertain memory
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The cartoon appeared on March 29, 1890, in the same month Bismarck left office.

options.text: It was commissioned by the German government to justify the removal of its chancellor
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or context suggests German sponsorship. It was published in a British magazine.

options.text: It shows both men in nautical clothing although neither of them served in the German navy
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The nautical dress is a deliberate ship-of-state metaphor. It does not limit what the cartoon reveals about attitudes.

facts: Punch was a British satirical magazine published in London.
Bismarck left office in March 1890.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line and context identify a British cartoonist and the British magazine Punch.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Acton's main claim about the declaration of rights in the excerpt?

options.text: The revolutionaries guarded against royal and noble power but left individuals exposed to an unchecked popular majority.
options.label: key
options.why: Acton says people were protected from 'government by authority or by minority' but 'made the majority irresistible,' so the real danger came from democracy itself.

options.text: The declaration failed because its authors deliberately strengthened the monarchy and aristocracy against popular demands for reform.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton says the people were 'resolved to be oppressed no more by monarchy or aristocracy,' which is the opposite of strengthening them.

options.text: The declaration should have been abandoned because any written guarantee of individual rights inevitably produces tyranny by the state.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Acton calls the declaration 'more needful still,' so he values it; his complaint is that it did not guard against majority rule.

options.text: European revolutions of the eighteenth century all followed one path, from constitutional monarchy to military dictatorship under a general.
options.label: too_broad
options.why: The excerpt is about France and the danger of majority rule, not a general pattern for every European revolution.

facts: The National Constituent Assembly adopted the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen in August 1789.
The Declaration rejected privileges based on birth and placed sovereignty in the nation.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton contrasts protection from monarchy and minority with the lack of any protection against an 'irresistible' majority.
design.evidence_quote: They were protected from government by authority or by minority; but they made the majority irresistible, and the plebiscite a tyranny.

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support Acton's claim that revolutionary France made 'the plebiscite a tyranny'?

options.text: Napoleon held plebiscites to gain popular approval for his rule as consul and later for his title of emperor.
options.label: key
options.why: Napoleon's plebiscites of 1800, 1802, and 1804 used popular votes to approve concentrated, authoritarian power, which matches Acton's point.

options.text: The Constitution of 1791 limited voting to active citizens who paid a set level of taxes, keeping power with propertied men.
options.label: reversal
options.why: A property qualification restricted majority rule, so it would weaken rather than support a claim about an all-powerful majority.

options.text: On the night of August 4, 1789, the National Assembly abolished feudal dues and many privileges held by the nobility and clergy.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This was a real event, but it concerns the 'dangers going out' (aristocratic privilege), not oppression by popular vote.

options.text: At the Congress of Vienna in 1815, the great powers restored legitimate monarchs and built a balance of power across Europe.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Vienna settlement restored monarchical legitimacy and did not use plebiscites to justify power.

facts: Napoleon used plebiscites to approve the Constitution of the Year VIII (1800), the life consulate (1802), and the imperial title (1804).
Napoleon was crowned emperor in 1804.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton's phrase about the plebiscite becoming a tyranny is best supported by Napoleon's use of popular votes to legitimize his rule.
design.evidence_quote: they made the majority irresistible, and the plebiscite a tyranny.

items.stem: Acton's concern about 'the collected will of the people' is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty, such as Rousseau's general will, that shaped revolutionary politics
options.label: key
options.why: Rousseau's Social Contract (1762) set out the general will, and the Declaration located sovereignty in the nation, the idea Acton worries left the individual unprotected.

options.text: Divine-right absolutism as defended by Bossuet, which held that kings answered to God alone and not to their subjects
options.label: reversal
options.why: Divine-right theory is the older royal 'authority' Acton says the revolutionaries had already guarded against, not the new danger of popular will.

options.text: Mercantilist theory, which held that governments should regulate trade and accumulate bullion to build national power
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Mercantilism concerned economic policy, not the political problem of a majority overriding individual rights.

options.text: The Scientific Revolution's stress on empirical observation, which led reformers to treat laws as experiments to be tested
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Empirical method shaped Enlightenment thought generally but is not the source of the idea of a collective popular will.

facts: Rousseau published The Social Contract in 1762, arguing that legitimate authority rests on the general will.
The 1789 Declaration stated that sovereignty resides essentially in the nation.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton's reference to the 'collected will of the people' ties to Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty and the general will.
design.evidence_quote: No European knew what security could be needed or provided for the individual from the collected will of the people.

items.stem: The fact that Acton gave these lectures in the 1890s is significant for interpreting the excerpt because it most likely

options.text: allowed him to judge the ideals of 1789 in light of later events such as the Terror and Napoleon's rule
options.label: key
options.why: Writing a century later, Acton knew of the Terror (1793-1794) and Napoleon's regime (1799-1815), which shaped his view of where majority rule led; this hindsight is also a limit when using him to explain what people in 1789 intended.

options.text: made his lectures an eyewitness record of the debates held in the National Assembly during the summer of 1789
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The credit line dates the lectures to 1895-1899, so Acton could not have witnessed the 1789 debates.

options.text: indicates he prepared the lectures as propaganda for the Committee of Public Safety during the radical phase of the Revolution
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Committee of Public Safety ruled in 1793-1794, about a century before Acton lectured.

options.text: proves he rejected every form of representative government, including the British Parliament under which he lived and taught
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt criticizes an unchecked majority, not representative government in general.

facts: The Reign of Terror lasted roughly from 1793 to 1794.
Napoleon held power in France from 1799 to 1815.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line and context line place the lectures in the 1890s, about a century after the events.

items.stem: Which of the following developments of 1793-1794 most directly illustrates the danger Acton describes of a 'new enemy, the State'?

options.text: The Committee of Public Safety used the Law of Suspects to arrest people as enemies of the republic.
options.label: key
options.why: During the Terror, a government claiming to speak for the people used the Law of Suspects (1793) to detain many people, showing state power used against individuals in the people's name.

options.text: The National Convention voted in 1794 to abolish slavery in France's Caribbean colonies, including Saint-Domingue.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Abolition in 1794 was real but extended rights rather than showing majority oppression of individuals.

options.text: In July 1794 the Thermidorian Reaction overthrew Robespierre and began dismantling the emergency revolutionary government.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Thermidor ended the Terror, so it was a reaction against the danger Acton describes, not an example of it.

options.text: Toussaint Louverture led a revolt of enslaved people in Saint-Domingue that became a war for Haitian independence.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Haitian Revolution was a colonial uprising against slavery, not an example of the French state using majority rule against individuals.

facts: The National Convention passed the Law of Suspects in September 1793.
Robespierre fell in the Thermidorian Reaction of July 1794.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton's warning that the state, acting for the people, became a new threat to individuals connects to the Terror's Law of Suspects.
design.evidence_quote: The classes were to be harmless; but there was the new enemy, the State.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Acton's argument in the excerpt about the origins of Portuguese exploration?

options.text: Geography pushed Portugal toward the sea, but individual initiative such as Henry's, not the state, drove exploration.
options.label: key
options.why: Acton says Portugal was shut in by Spain with no opening but the Atlantic, and that exploration did not come from the State but from the interests of Prince Henry.

options.text: The Portuguese crown directed exploration as a centralized state enterprise, planning and financing each voyage from its court in Lisbon.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This reverses Acton's direct statement that the great national work of exploration did not proceed from the State.

options.text: Prince Henry earned his reputation by personally captaining voyages from Sagres to the coasts of West Africa and Asia.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton explicitly says Henry was not a navigator himself; he watched the ships from Sagres.

options.text: Crusading zeal to convert Muslims and Africans was the chief motive, outweighing any single geographic or political factor.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt mentions Henry's service in the African wars but stresses geography and politics; it never makes religious conversion the main cause.

facts: Prince Henry of Portugal (1394-1460) sponsored voyages along the West African coast in the fifteenth century.
Portugal borders Spain on land and faces the Atlantic Ocean.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton links Portugal's Atlantic turn to being hemmed in by Spain and then says exploration did not come from the State but from Henry's interest.
design.evidence_quote: The great national work of exploration did not proceed from the State.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the Portuguese ships Acton describes were able to make long voyages down the African coast in the fifteenth century?

options.text: Caravels combining square and lateen sails, along with tools such as the magnetic compass and astrolabe
options.label: key
options.why: Portuguese caravels could sail against the wind and handle Atlantic conditions, and navigators used the compass and astrolabe to find direction and latitude.

options.text: Marine chronometers that let captains fix longitude precisely, allowing safe return voyages across the open Atlantic
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Reliable marine chronometers for finding longitude came in the eighteenth century, long after Henry's time.

options.text: Oared galleys with large crews, the same Mediterranean vessels that let Venice dominate the eastern spice trade
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Galleys did serve Mediterranean powers, but they were unsuited to long Atlantic voyages and were not what made Portuguese exploration possible.

options.text: Mercator's printed world map projection, which gave Portuguese pilots reliable charts of the African coastline
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Mercator published his projection in 1569, more than a century after Henry's voyages started.

facts: The caravel, which used lateen sails, was developed and used by Portuguese explorers in the fifteenth century.
The magnetic compass and astrolabe were navigational tools used by Iberian sailors in the Age of Exploration.
Mercator's map projection was published in 1569.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton describes ships moving between the Tagus and the lands that would become the Portuguese empire; the question asks what technology made those voyages possible.
design.evidence_quote: he watched the ships that passed between the great maritime centre at the mouth of the Tagus

items.stem: Portuguese expansion along the African coast, as described in the excerpt, was most directly connected to which development of the 1500s?

options.text: The growth of a transatlantic trade in enslaved Africans to supply sugar plantations in Brazil
options.label: key
options.why: Portuguese trading posts on the African coast became bases for the trade in enslaved people, who were shipped to sugar plantations in Atlantic islands and Brazil during the sixteenth century.

options.text: The price revolution set off by massive shipments of silver that Portuguese fleets carried home from mines in Mexico and Peru
options.label: misattributed
options.why: American silver from Mexico and Peru flowed mainly to Spain, not Portugal.

options.text: The Dutch East India Company's chartering and its seizure of Portuguese spice outposts across the Indian Ocean
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602, and its attacks on Portuguese outposts happened in the seventeenth century.

options.text: The enclosure of common fields in England, which pushed rural laborers off the land and into the towns
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Enclosure was a change in English agriculture that had nothing to do with Portuguese expansion along the African coast.

facts: Portugal claimed Brazil after Cabral's landing in 1500 and developed sugar plantations there using enslaved Africans in the 1500s.
The Dutch East India Company was founded in 1602.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton mentions Henry's African wars and the regions that would make up the Portuguese empire, which ties the source to Portuguese Africa and the Atlantic trade that grew from it.
design.evidence_quote: the regions that were to compose the Portuguese empire

items.stem: EXTRA: Acton's description of the ocean as a universal waterway that unites mankind was most likely influenced by which feature of his own time?

options.text: A late-1800s world linked by steamships, telegraph cables, and European empires
options.label: key
options.why: Acton lectured around 1899, when steamships, undersea telegraph cables and the new imperialism had tied the world together. That setting fits his view of the ocean as something that joins humanity together.

options.text: The humanist revival of classical learning that inspired Renaissance scholars to study ancient geography
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Renaissance humanism belongs to the period Acton studied, not to the late nineteenth century in which he wrote.

options.text: The decolonization movements that dismantled Europe's overseas empires and created new independent states
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Decolonization happened mainly after 1945, decades after Acton's lectures.

options.text: The mercantilist belief that nations should close their colonial sea lanes to all foreign shipping
options.label: reversal
options.why: Closing sea lanes is the opposite of seeing the ocean as a waterway that unites mankind.

facts: Lord Acton lectured on modern history at Cambridge in the late 1890s.
By the late nineteenth century, undersea telegraph cables and steamships connected Europe with its overseas empires.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates the lecture to about 1899, and the opening sentence shows a view of the ocean as something that unites humanity.
design.evidence_quote: the ocean is not a limit, but the universal waterway that unites mankind

items.stem: EXTRA: Acton's reference to the growing absolutism of the Portuguese dynasty places fifteenth-century Portugal within which broader European development?

options.text: New monarchs strengthening royal authority at the expense of the nobility
options.label: key
options.why: Acton describes nobles shut out of politics by a strengthening dynasty. This matches the New Monarchies of the period, such as Henry VII in England and Ferdinand and Isabella in Spain, which limited the independence of the nobles.

options.text: Louis XIV's taming of the French nobility at Versailles in the late seventeenth century
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Louis XIV's court at Versailles came about two centuries after the Portuguese developments Acton describes.

options.text: The growing power of territorial princes who kept the Holy Roman emperor weak and divided
options.label: reversal
options.why: In the Holy Roman Empire, regional lords gained power at the expense of the center, which is the opposite of the trend Acton describes.

options.text: The Hanseatic League's control of Baltic trade by merchant cities independent of kings
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Hanseatic League was a commercial alliance of northern towns. It has nothing to do with a dynasty limiting its nobles.

facts: Henry VII (r. 1485-1509) strengthened royal power in England after the Wars of the Roses.
Ferdinand and Isabella strengthened royal authority over the Spanish nobility in the late fifteenth century.
Louis XIV moved his court to Versailles in 1682.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton says the territorial magnate was excluded from politics by the dynasty's growing absolutism, which fits the New Monarchies pattern.
design.evidence_quote: who was excluded from politics by the growing absolutism of the dynasty

items.stem: The excerpt states that the constitution "abolished the individual veto in parliament." This reform was intended mainly to

options.text: end a rule that let a single noble deputy block the Sejm's decisions
options.label: key
options.why: The liberum veto let any one deputy dissolve the Sejm and cancel its acts. It paralyzed government and gave foreign powers an easy way to manipulate it, so ending it was central to the 1791 reform.

options.text: strip the elected king of his right to reject laws passed by the Sejm's deputies
options.label: reversal
options.why: The veto belonged to individual noble deputies, not the king. The constitution actually strengthened the monarchy by making it hereditary.

options.text: abolish serfdom and grant peasants equal votes with nobles in the national parliament
options.label: overstated
options.why: The constitution did not abolish serfdom. The excerpt limits people's sovereignty to the noble and bourgeois classes.

options.text: replace the Sejm entirely with councils of ministers appointed by the new hereditary king
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes a separation of powers that kept a legislative branch. It does not describe abolishing the Sejm.

facts: Under the liberum veto, a single deputy could dissolve the Polish Sejm and void its legislation.
The Constitution of May 3, 1791 abolished the liberum veto and made the Polish monarchy hereditary.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names the abolition of the individual veto as a key reform of the 1791 constitution.
design.evidence_quote: The new constitution abolished the individual veto in parliament

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's argument about the effects of the first partition of 1772 on Poland-Lithuania?

options.text: It left Poland intact enough to survive and spurred support for government reform
options.label: key
options.why: The author says the partition did not threaten Poland's viability, since the heartland was kept, and that its shock created support for Enlightenment reform.

options.text: It destroyed the Polish heartland and left the Commonwealth unable to function as a state
options.label: reversal
options.why: The author says the opposite: Poland kept extensive territory, including the Polish heartland.

options.text: It was welcomed by King Stanislaw August as a chance to copy the Russian and Prussian models of absolutism
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The excerpt says the king promoted the ideas of Burke, Washington, and progressive reformers, not the absolutist models of the partitioning powers.

options.text: It united Polish nobles behind the old system, including the elected monarchy and the veto
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The author argues that the partition revealed the dangers of institutional decay and built opinion in favor of reform, not loyalty to the old system.

facts: Russia, Prussia, and Austria carried out the first partition of Poland-Lithuania in 1772.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The opening sentences say the 1772 partition did not threaten Poland's viability and that its shock created a pro-reform body of opinion.
design.evidence_quote: the shock of the annexations made clear the dangers of decay in government institutions, creating a body of opinion favorable to reform

items.stem: The constitution described in the excerpt is best understood as part of which broader development of the late eighteenth century?

options.text: Enlightenment ideas inspiring written constitutions during an age of Atlantic revolutions
options.label: key
options.why: The 1791 constitution came soon after the United States Constitution and during the early French Revolution. The excerpt links it to Montesquieu, Rousseau, and the American document.

options.text: Liberal and nationalist uprisings that swept the German states, Italy, and the Austrian Empire in 1848
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The revolutions of 1848 came more than half a century after the 1791 constitution.

options.text: Mercantilist competition among European powers for colonial trade in the Caribbean and India
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Colonial trade rivalry was real in this period, but it has nothing to do with Polish constitutional reform.

options.text: Enlightened absolutist rulers such as Catherine II centralizing power without written constitutions
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Enlightened absolutism was a real development, but the Polish constitution was a parliamentary product that separated powers. It was not a ruler's unilateral centralization.

facts: The United States Constitution was drafted in 1787.
The French Revolution began in 1789, and France adopted a written constitution in 1791.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt ties the constitution to Enlightenment philosophers and to the contemporaneous United States document.
design.evidence_quote: Conceived in the liberal spirit of the contemporaneous document in the United States

items.stem: Which of the following was a direct result, within the next five years, of the reforms described in the excerpt?

options.text: Russian intervention and two further partitions ended Poland-Lithuania's existence by 1795
options.label: key
options.why: Russia invaded in 1792 to overturn the reforms. Russia and Prussia then partitioned Poland in 1793, and after the defeat of Kosciuszko's uprising, the third partition of 1795 ended the state.

options.text: Prussia honored its 1790 alliance with Poland and sent armies to defend the constitution against Russia
options.label: reversal
options.why: Prussia abandoned Poland and joined Russia in the second partition of 1793.

options.text: Napoleon restored the full Commonwealth and its constitution of 1791 as the Duchy of Warsaw
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Duchy of Warsaw was created in 1807, well outside the five-year window. It was also a smaller French client state, not a restored Commonwealth.

options.text: Austria alone annexed the remaining Polish lands after crushing a peasant revolt in Galicia
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The final partition was shared by Russia, Prussia, and Austria. The well-known Galician peasant revolt came in 1846.

facts: Russia and Prussia carried out the second partition of Poland in 1793.
Russia, Prussia, and Austria carried out the third partition in 1795, ending the Polish-Lithuanian state.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt ends with the 1791 constitution; students must connect these reforms to the neighboring powers' response and the partitions that followed.
design.evidence_quote: Stanislaw August's process of renovation reached its climax on May 3, 1791

items.stem: Which of the following developments would best support the author's claim that the first partition created opinion favorable to reform along Enlightenment lines?

options.text: The Sejm's 1773 creation of a Commission of National Education to oversee state schooling
options.label: key
options.why: The Commission was created the year after the first partition and reformed schooling along Enlightenment lines. This is direct evidence that the partition was followed by a push for reform.

options.text: The Bar Confederation's armed defense of Catholic privileges and noble liberties against Russia in 1768
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Bar Confederation came before the 1772 partition and defended traditional privileges, so it cannot show reform opinion arising after the partition.

options.text: Catherine II's issuing of the Nakaz, her instruction to a Russian legislative commission, in 1767
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Nakaz was a real Enlightenment-influenced document, but it was Russian and came before the partition, so it says nothing about Polish opinion after 1772.

options.text: The Targowica Confederation of 1792, in which magnates asked Russia to help overturn the new constitution
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Targowica Confederation was organized against the reforms, so it would weaken rather than support the claim of growing reform opinion.

facts: The Commission of National Education was established in Poland-Lithuania in 1773.
The Targowica Confederation was formed in 1792 to overturn the May 3 Constitution with Russian support.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The author claims that the shock of 1772 produced pro-reform opinion inspired by the Enlightenment; a reform enacted in 1773 supports that claim.
design.evidence_quote: creating a body of opinion favorable to reform along the lines of the European Enlightenment

items.stem: The declaration's promise of free elections and governments responsive to the will of the people most directly reflects which earlier development?

options.text: Wartime Allied pledges, such as the Atlantic Charter, to respect national self-determination
options.label: key
options.why: The 1941 Atlantic Charter affirmed the right of peoples to choose their form of government. The declaration applies that principle to liberated Europe by promising free elections.

options.text: The Treaty of Versailles requirement that the defeated Central Powers adopt democratic constitutions
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Versailles imposed territorial losses, disarmament and reparations. It did not require the defeated states to adopt democratic constitutions.

options.text: The Comintern's call for workers in occupied countries to set up soviet-style councils after their liberation
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Comintern was dissolved in 1943. Soviet-style councils are also the opposite of the multiparty free elections the declaration promises.

options.text: The Munich Agreement's guarantee that the remaining territory of Czechoslovakia would hold free elections
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1938 Munich Agreement gave the Sudetenland to Germany. It said nothing about guaranteeing free elections.

facts: Roosevelt and Churchill issued the Atlantic Charter in August 1941, affirming the right of peoples to choose their own form of government.
The Munich Agreement of 1938 transferred the Sudetenland to Germany.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The pledge of free elections and representative interim governments echoes the self-determination principles of the Atlantic Charter.
design.evidence_quote: through free elections of Governments responsive to the will of the people

items.stem: Based on its authorship and content, the declaration was most likely intended to

options.text: display Allied unity and promise liberated peoples a voice in choosing their governments
options.label: key
options.why: All three leaders signed this joint statement. It stresses their mutual agreement and promises democratic means and free elections for liberated peoples.

options.text: announce the terms under which Nazi Germany had agreed to an unconditional surrender to the three powers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Germany did not surrender until May 1945, three months after the declaration was issued.

options.text: launch a joint American-funded program of reconstruction loans like the later Marshall Plan
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Marshall Plan began in 1948, and the Soviet Union refused to take part. The declaration mentions emergency relief, not a program of loans.

options.text: warn the Soviet Union that the Western powers would resist any expansion of communism into eastern Europe
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Stalin was one of the declaration's authors. The text presents a shared agreement, not a Western warning aimed at the Soviet Union.

facts: The Yalta Conference of February 1945 brought together Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill.
Germany surrendered unconditionally in May 1945.
The Marshall Plan began in 1948.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The joint authorship and the language of mutual agreement and democratic means show that the declaration aimed to present a united Allied pledge.
design.evidence_quote: They jointly declare their mutual agreement to concert during the temporary period of instability in liberated Europe

items.stem: Which military situation in early 1945 most directly shaped the leaders' concern with the political future of liberated Europe?

options.text: Soviet armies had pushed German forces out of most of Poland and much of eastern Europe
options.label: key
options.why: By February 1945 the Red Army held Poland and much of eastern Europe. That made it urgent to decide what kind of governments these liberated states would have.

options.text: The Western Allies had not yet opened a second front in France, leaving the Soviets to fight Germany alone
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Western Allies landed in Normandy in June 1944, months before Yalta.

options.text: Germany had already surrendered and been divided into four occupation zones administered by the Allies
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Germany surrendered in May 1945, after Yalta. The occupation came after the surrender.

options.text: The United States had ended the Pacific war by dropping atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The atomic bombings happened in August 1945, six months after the declaration.

facts: The Red Army captured Warsaw in January 1945.
The Allied landings in Normandy took place in June 1944.
The atomic bombs were dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki in August 1945.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The repeated references to liberated Europe and to former Axis satellite states point to the Soviet advance through eastern Europe.
design.evidence_quote: the peoples of the former Axis satellite states of Europe

items.stem: Which of the following best describes how political developments in eastern Europe between 1945 and 1948 related to the promises made in the declaration?

options.text: Soviet-backed communists took power, contradicting the pledge of free elections
options.label: key
options.why: By 1948, for example through the Czechoslovak coup, Soviet-backed communist parties controlled eastern Europe. This undercut the declaration's promise of free elections and deepened Cold War divisions.

options.text: Free elections produced stable multiparty governments that kept eastern Europe neutral in the Cold War
options.label: reversal
options.why: Eastern Europe became a bloc of Soviet satellite states, not a neutral group of multiparty democracies.

options.text: Western powers enforced the pledge by stationing NATO troops in Poland and Czechoslovakia to supervise voting
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: NATO was founded in 1949, and no Western troops supervised elections in the Soviet sphere. Poland and the Czech Republic joined NATO only in 1999.

options.text: Eastern European states joined the European Economic Community to secure Western aid for elections
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The EEC was created in 1957. Eastern European states joined its successor, the European Union, only after the fall of communism.

facts: Communists took full power in Czechoslovakia in a coup in February 1948.
NATO was founded in 1949.
The European Economic Community was created by the Treaty of Rome in 1957.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The pledge to hold free elections is the promise that the communist takeovers of 1945 to 1948 contradicted.
design.evidence_quote: to facilitate where necessary the holding of such elections

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following most limits the usefulness of the declaration as evidence of the three leaders' actual postwar intentions?

options.text: As a joint public pledge, it may mask real disagreements among the leaders over Poland
options.label: key
options.why: A jointly signed public statement shows only what the three leaders agreed to say. Their sharp disagreements over Poland's postwar government do not appear in it, and the phrase about their own judgment left room for differing interpretations.

options.text: It was drafted by Soviet officials alone and so reflects only the communist view of postwar Europe
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line states that the Soviet, British and American leaders issued the statement together.

options.text: It was written after the war ended and so describes completed outcomes rather than future plans
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The declaration was issued in February 1945, while the war in Europe was still going on, and it speaks of future intentions.

options.text: It was kept secret until the 1990s, so it could not have influenced public opinion during the war
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the provenance suggests the declaration was secret. It was published shortly after the conference ended.

facts: At Yalta in 1945, the three leaders disagreed over the composition of Poland's postwar government.
The Yalta Conference ended on February 11, 1945, before Germany's surrender.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The declaration is a joint public statement, and its qualifying phrase leaves the conditions for joint action to the powers' own discretion.
design.evidence_quote: where, in their judgment conditions require

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following best describes the main commitment the three leaders make in the excerpt?

options.text: To jointly help liberated states hold free elections for representative governments
options.label: key
options.why: The leaders promise to assist jointly in forming broadly representative interim authorities and in holding free elections.

options.text: To let each power separately administer the countries its own armies had freed from German control
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt repeatedly stresses joint action by the three governments, not separate control by each power.

options.text: To exclude the former Axis satellite states from any role in the postwar political settlement of Europe
options.label: reversal
options.why: The text explicitly includes the peoples of the former Axis satellite states among those to be assisted.

options.text: To require liberated states to adopt the economic system of the power that had liberated them
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt calls for solving problems by democratic means and does not mention imposing any economic system.

facts: The Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe was issued on February 11, 1945, by the Soviet, British and American leaders.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Points (c) and (d) commit the three governments to assist in forming representative interim governments and holding free elections.
design.evidence_quote: to form interim governmental authorities broadly representative of all democratic elements in the population

items.stem: Sassoon's point of view in the poem was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: His service as an officer who saw heavy losses among the men he led at the front
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says Sassoon was a British officer on the Western Front. His bitterness toward the comfortable men at the Base comes from watching front-line soldiers die in large numbers.

options.text: His commitment to the Bolshevik program of turning the imperialist war into a class revolution across Europe
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The poem's target is staff officers, not capitalism. Nothing in it reflects Bolshevik revolutionary theory, so this outlook belongs to Lenin and not to Sassoon.

options.text: His work as a government propagandist assigned to build civilian support for the war effort at home
options.label: reversal
options.why: The poem mocks the war's leadership rather than promoting the war. The context line also describes Sassoon as a front-line officer, not a propagandist.

options.text: His conviction, shared by most British writers in August 1914, that the war would be brief and glorious
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Hopes for a short, glorious war belong to 1914. By 1917 Sassoon was expressing disillusionment, the opposite attitude.

facts: Siegfried Sassoon served as a British infantry officer on the Western Front during the First World War.
Sassoon wrote Base Details in 1917, and it was published in Counter-Attack and Other Poems in 1918.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line identifies the author as a British officer who served on the Western Front, and the poem contrasts the Base with soldiers going 'up the line to death'.
design.evidence_quote: Siegfried Sassoon was a British army officer who served on the Western Front

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim of the poem?

options.text: Senior officers behind the lines lived comfortably while sending young soldiers to die
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker imagines himself as a staff officer at the Base, eating in the best hotel and sending 'glum heroes up the line to death' while staying safe himself.

options.text: Staff officers shared the dangers of the trenches and grieved deeply for the soldiers they lost
options.label: reversal
options.why: The poem says the opposite. The officers stay safe and 'die--in bed', and their 'Poor young chap' is a shallow response, not deep grief.

options.text: Britain should open immediate peace negotiations with Germany on the basis of the territorial status quo
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The poem does not propose any diplomatic solution or peace terms. It is a satire of the army's command.

options.text: The war was caused mainly by the alliance diplomacy of aging aristocrats in the European capitals
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The poem does not discuss what caused the war. It is about how the war was being run and who paid the price.

facts: During the First World War, British staff officers usually worked at headquarters and bases well behind the front line, and their red tabs gave them the nickname 'red tabs'.
Front-line British infantry suffered very heavy casualties in Western Front offensives in 1916 and 1917.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The poem sets the comfortable life of the 'scarlet Majors at the Base' against the deaths of the young men they send to the front.
design.evidence_quote: I'd live with scarlet Majors at the Base, And speed glum heroes up the line to death.

items.stem: Which of the following aspects of the First World War provides the most direct context for the poem's reference to soldiers sent "up the line to death"?

options.text: Repeated costly offensives against entrenched positions on the Western Front
options.label: key
options.why: By 1917, offensives such as the Somme (1916) and Passchendaele (1917) had produced huge British losses for little ground gained. This is the slaughter the poem blames on the men at the Base.

options.text: The rapid German advance through Belgium toward Paris in the opening weeks of the war
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The war of movement in 1914 ended at the Marne. The poem, written in 1917, reflects the trench stalemate that followed.

options.text: The German campaign of unrestricted submarine warfare against Allied and neutral shipping
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Unrestricted submarine warfare did take place in 1917, but it was a naval campaign. It does not explain soldiers being sent 'up the line' on land.

options.text: The collapse of the Russian army and Russia's withdrawal from the war after the Bolshevik takeover
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Russia's withdrawal at Brest-Litovsk in 1918 happened on the Eastern Front. It has nothing to do with British soldiers being sent to the trenches.

facts: The British army suffered about 57,000 casualties on the first day of the Battle of the Somme, 1 July 1916.
The Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele) was fought from July to November 1917 and gained little ground at great cost.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The phrase 'up the line' refers to front-line trenches, and the speaker mentions the 'Roll of Honour' and losing 'heavily in this last scrap'. Together these point to costly trench offensives.
design.evidence_quote: Yes, we've lost heavily in this last scrap.

items.stem: The attitude toward the war expressed in the poem was most similar to which of the following developments in the interwar period?

options.text: Novels such as Remarque's All Quiet on the Western Front depicting the war as futile
options.label: key
options.why: Like Sassoon's satire, Remarque's 1929 novel showed ordinary soldiers sacrificed for nothing. It was part of a wider postwar literature of disillusionment.

options.text: Futurist manifestos praising war as the only hygiene of the world and the path to modern renewal
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Futurism glorified war, and Marinetti's manifesto came out in 1909, before the war. It is neither interwar nor similar to Sassoon's view.

options.text: Fascist movements that celebrated the frontline comradeship of veterans as a model for the nation
options.label: reversal
options.why: Fascists turned war experience into a heroic myth, while Sassoon's poem rejects the heroic language of the war.

options.text: Soviet socialist realism requiring artists to portray heroic workers building a socialist society
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Socialist realism was a state-imposed style about building socialism. It was not a response to soldiers' disillusionment with the First World War.

facts: Erich Maria Remarque published All Quiet on the Western Front in 1929.
F. T. Marinetti published the Futurist Manifesto in 1909.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The poem's bitter final line about youth 'stone dead' while officers die in bed expresses the disillusionment later found in interwar antiwar literature.
design.evidence_quote: And when the war is done and youth stone dead, I'd toddle safely home and die--in bed.

items.stem: Which of the following is a limitation of the poem as evidence about how British staff officers actually behaved during the war?

options.text: As satire, it uses an exaggerated caricature rather than an account of specific officers
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker is an imagined 'fierce, and bald' major with a 'puffy petulant face'. This is a deliberate caricature, so it shows front-line resentment better than it shows the documented conduct of real staff officers.

options.text: It was written after the armistice and so reflects hindsight about the war's final outcome
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The credit line dates the poem to 1917, before the armistice of November 1918.

options.text: Its author served only in Britain and lacked any direct experience of conditions on the Western Front
options.label: reversal
options.why: The context line states that Sassoon served on the Western Front.

options.text: It was commissioned by the War Office, so it presents the official government view of the army command
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the provenance suggests the government commissioned it. Its harsh mockery of officers is the opposite of an official view.

facts: The armistice ending fighting on the Western Front took effect on 11 November 1918.
Sassoon wrote Base Details in 1917, while the war was still being fought.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The poem is written in the conditional ('If I were'), and the speaker is an invented, exaggerated figure rather than a named officer. That makes it satire, not documentation.
design.evidence_quote: If I were fierce, and bald, and short of breath

items.stem: Which of the following is most likely a limitation of Bourrienne's memoirs as a source for Napoleon's exact reasons for the Concordat?

options.text: He wrote nearly three decades later, so the quoted words may be reconstructed from memory rather than recorded exactly.
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the memoirs came out in 1829 and describe events of 1801. A direct quotation written down 28 years later may be reconstructed or shaped after the fact.

options.text: He published while Napoleon still ruled France, so imperial censors probably required him to portray the First Consul as wise and moderate.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The context line says the memoirs appeared in 1829, after Napoleon's death in 1821. No imperial censor was involved.

options.text: He served as a papal envoy during the negotiations, so he likely exaggerated how much Napoleon valued the Catholic Church in France.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Bourrienne was Napoleon's private secretary, not a papal diplomat.

options.text: He relied entirely on rumors reported by others, since he had no personal access to Napoleon during the period of the Concordat talks.
options.label: reversal
options.why: As private secretary until 1802, Bourrienne had close personal access to Napoleon in 1801.

facts: The Concordat between Napoleon and Pope Pius VII was signed in 1801.
Napoleon died in 1821, and Bourrienne's memoirs were published in 1829.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line gives the 1829 publication date and says the passage describes events of 1801, a gap of nearly three decades.

items.stem: In the excerpt, Napoleon argues that

options.text: restoring Catholicism while allowing minority worship would prevent religious strife and satisfy most of the French
options.label: key
options.why: Napoleon says he dreads religious quarrels. He claims that reviving the majority religion while giving the minority freedom of worship will satisfy everyone.

options.text: creating a separate Gallican Church headed from within France would raise his authority to that of the first Roman emperors
options.label: reversal
options.why: This was the argument of the party urging him to break with the Pope. The excerpt says Napoleon's ideas did not agree with theirs.

options.text: encouraging the spread of Protestantism across France would weaken papal influence and bind the people more closely to the state
options.label: reversal
options.why: Napoleon does say part of France might turn Protestant, but he treats this as a danger that would cause schism and conflict, not as a goal.

options.text: the Catholic clergy must first recover the Church lands sold during the Revolution before any settlement with Rome could last
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not mention Church lands. In fact, the Concordat accepted the sale of those lands.

facts: In the 1801 Concordat the papacy accepted the loss of Church lands confiscated during the Revolution.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Napoleon's closing sentence pairs reviving the prevailing religion with freedom of worship for the minority, and says this will satisfy everyone.
design.evidence_quote: In, reviving a religion which has always prevailed in the country... and in giving the liberty of exercising their worship to the minority, I shall satisfy every one.

items.stem: The religious settlement Napoleon describes in the excerpt was most directly related to earlier revolutionary policy in which of the following ways?

options.text: It sought to heal the split created by the Civil Constitution of the Clergy between juring and nonjuring priests.
options.label: key
options.why: The 1790 Civil Constitution of the Clergy, together with its required oath, split the French clergy and turned many Catholics against the Revolution. The Concordat aimed to reconcile the Church with the state.

options.text: It returned to the Church all of the lands that the National Assembly had confiscated and sold off as biens nationaux in 1789-1790.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Concordat did the opposite: the papacy accepted that the confiscated lands would not be returned.

options.text: It made the Cult of the Supreme Being, first promoted by Robespierre in 1794, the official civic religion of the French Republic.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Napoleon revived Catholicism. The Cult of the Supreme Being collapsed after Robespierre's fall in 1794.

options.text: It continued the policy of the Revocation of the Edict of Nantes by outlawing Protestant worship throughout France.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Revocation dates from 1685 under Louis XIV. Napoleon also promises the minority freedom of worship, which contradicts this option.

facts: The National Assembly passed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy in 1790, and the clerical oath that followed split priests into jurors and nonjurors.
Robespierre held the Festival of the Supreme Being in 1794.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Napoleon's aim of 'reviving' a religion that 'still prevails in the hearts of the people' points to reversing the earlier revolutionary break with the Church.
design.evidence_quote: reviving a religion which has always prevailed in the country, and which still prevails in the hearts of the people

items.stem: Napoleon's fear of religious quarrels and public distractions in 1801 is best understood in the context of

options.text: Catholic anger at revolutionary religious policy, which had helped fuel revolts such as the uprising in the Vendée
options.label: key
options.why: Religious grievances helped drive counterrevolutionary revolts such as the Vendée uprising of 1793. Napoleon wanted to remove this source of internal division.

options.text: the sixteenth-century Wars of Religion, during which Catholic and Huguenot nobles fought for control of the French monarchy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These wars ended in the 1590s. They are not the immediate context for a policy made in 1801.

options.text: the Kulturkampf campaign, in which a newly unified state sought to curb the political influence of the Catholic clergy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Kulturkampf took place in Bismarck's Germany in the 1870s, long after 1801.

options.text: the Jansenist controversy, in which Louis XIV and the papacy jointly suppressed a strict Catholic movement at Port-Royal
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This conflict was real, but it belonged to the reign of Louis XIV and does not explain the revolutionary-era tensions Napoleon faced.

facts: A Catholic and royalist revolt broke out in the Vendée in 1793.
Napoleon became First Consul after the coup of Brumaire in 1799.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Napoleon says he dreads religious quarrels and family dissensions. That fear reflects the religious divisions the Revolution had produced.
design.evidence_quote: I dread the religious quarrels, the family dissensions, and the public distractions

items.stem: Napoleon's plan to revive Catholicism while giving the minority liberty of worship best reflects which broader feature of his rule?

options.text: He kept some revolutionary gains, such as religious toleration, while restoring order and authority
options.label: key
options.why: Napoleon combined authoritarian order with some revolutionary principles, including toleration and legal equality, as in the Civil Code of 1804. The excerpt's pairing of Catholic revival with minority worship shows the same balance.

options.text: He restored the legal privileges of the First Estate, including exemption from taxes and the collection of the tithe
options.label: reversal
options.why: Napoleon did not restore the clergy's privileges from before 1789 or the tithe. The Concordat made clergy salaried by the state.

options.text: He adopted the Enlightenment deists' rejection of organized religion and sought to eliminate churches from public life
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt shows Napoleon reviving an organized church, not removing churches from public life.

options.text: He placed the French state and its clergy under full papal authority, renouncing any government role in naming bishops
options.label: overstated
options.why: Under the Concordat the First Consul nominated bishops and the Pope invested them, so the state kept considerable control.

facts: Under the 1801 Concordat the First Consul nominated bishops, the Pope gave them canonical investiture, and the state paid clergy salaries.
The Napoleonic Civil Code of 1804 affirmed equality before the law.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The closing sentence pairs restoring the majority religion with freedom of worship for the minority, which combines restoration with a revolutionary principle.
design.evidence_quote: giving the liberty of exercising their worship to the minority

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim of the excerpt about Soviet policy toward Eastern Europe in the mid- to late 1980s?

options.text: Moscow still sought strong influence in Eastern Europe but relied less on force to keep it
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt says the basic policy of keeping a high level of influence was unchanged, but the means shifted from coercion toward political and economic instruments.

options.text: Moscow had given up its interest in Eastern Europe and let each bloc state set its own course freely
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt states the policy of maintaining a high level of influence had not been altered.

options.text: All six East European leaders welcomed perestroika and glasnost and copied the Soviet reforms at home
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt says East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Romania resisted far-reaching reforms.

options.text: Moscow kept its bloc together mainly by threatening armed intervention like that in Prague in 1968
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt describes a shift away from coercion, the opposite of reliance on military threats.

facts: Mikhail Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 and promoted perestroika and glasnost.
Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia in 1968.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The final sentence contrasts the unchanged goal of influence with the changed, less coercive means.
design.evidence_quote: the nature of Soviet influence apparently had shifted away from coercion toward political and economic instruments of influence

items.stem: The Soviet shift away from coercion in Eastern Europe described in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Soviet economic stagnation, made worse by arms race spending and the costly war in Afghanistan
options.label: key
options.why: By the 1980s the Soviet economy was stagnating and burdened by military spending and the war in Afghanistan (1979-1989), which made coercive control of the bloc more costly and pushed Gorbachev toward reform.

options.text: The arrival of Marshall Plan aid, which tied East European economies more closely to Western markets and banks
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Marshall Plan aid began in 1948 and was refused by the Soviet bloc under Moscow's pressure.

options.text: Khrushchev's 1956 Secret Speech denouncing Stalin, which ended the use of Soviet troops to control the bloc
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Secret Speech came decades earlier, and Soviet troops crushed the Hungarian uprising later that same year.

options.text: The Maastricht Treaty's creation of the European Union, which drew Warsaw Pact states into Western trade
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992, after the period the excerpt describes and after the Warsaw Pact dissolved.

facts: The Soviet Union fought in Afghanistan from 1979 to 1989.
The Soviet economy experienced prolonged stagnation in the 1970s and 1980s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's reference to a move from coercion to political and economic tools under Gorbachev's reform agenda is the development students must place in context.
design.evidence_quote: shifted away from coercion toward political and economic instruments of influence

items.stem: The leaders' support for reform in Poland and Hungary described in the excerpt is most directly connected to which of the following developments in 1989?

options.text: Negotiated change, such as Round Table talks with Solidarity that led to partly free elections
options.label: key
options.why: In Poland, Round Table talks in early 1989 led to the June 1989 elections that Solidarity won, and Hungary also moved toward a negotiated transition; reform-minded leaders made a peaceful handover possible.

options.text: A violent uprising in which army units joined protesters and the ruling leader and his wife were executed
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes Romania in December 1989, a state the excerpt lists among those whose leaders resisted reform.

options.text: Soviet tanks entering their capitals to crush reformers as they had done in Budapest in 1956 and Prague in 1968
options.label: reversal
options.why: The USSR did not intervene in 1989, which fits the shift away from coercion the excerpt describes.

options.text: Their immediate admission as full members of the European Union and NATO in the same year as the reforms
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Poland and Hungary joined NATO in 1999 and the EU in 2004, not in 1989.

facts: Polish Round Table talks between the government and Solidarity took place in 1989, followed by partly free elections in June 1989.
Nicolae Ceausescu was executed in December 1989.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names Poland and Hungary as states whose leaders supported Gorbachev's reforms.
design.evidence_quote: The leaders of Poland, Hungary, and Bulgaria apparently supported Gorbachev's reforms

items.stem: Which of the following most limits a historian's use of the excerpt as evidence about the end of communist rule in Eastern Europe?

options.text: It was finished before most bloc regimes fell, so it could not show how the reforms turned out
options.label: key
options.why: The credit line says research was completed in 1989, before the late-1989 revolutions and the 1991 Soviet collapse, so the study cannot assess their outcome.

options.text: As an official Soviet publication it likely exaggerated East European enthusiasm for Gorbachev's program
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The credit and context lines identify it as a U.S. Library of Congress study, not a Soviet publication.

options.text: Its authors were East European dissidents who wanted to discredit the communist leaders they named
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the provenance identifies the authors as dissidents; it was prepared for the U.S. government.

options.text: It relied mainly on Gorbachev's own memoirs, so it repeats his account of why the bloc changed course
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Gorbachev's memoirs appeared in the mid-1990s, after this study was completed.

facts: Communist regimes in East Germany, Czechoslovakia, and Romania fell in late 1989.
The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line states research was completed in 1989, and the excerpt speaks only of the mid- to late 1980s.

items.stem: The policy of glasnost mentioned in the excerpt is best explained as

options.text: Greater openness that eased censorship and allowed public criticism of officials
options.label: key
options.why: Glasnost meant openness: relaxed censorship and freer public discussion of Soviet problems and history.

options.text: Economic restructuring that let some private cooperatives operate and gave factories more autonomy
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This describes perestroika, the companion policy named in the same sentence.

options.text: A return to Lenin's New Economic Policy that allowed peasants to sell their grain surplus on open markets
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The NEP dates from the 1920s, not the 1980s.

options.text: A program of rapid heavy industrialization directed by five-year plans and enforced by the secret police
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes Stalin's policies beginning in 1928.

facts: Gorbachev introduced glasnost in the mid-1980s, relaxing censorship.
Perestroika (restructuring) allowed limited private cooperatives from 1988.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names glasnost as part of Gorbachev's reform emphasis at home and in Eastern Europe.
design.evidence_quote: Gorbachev's emphasis on perestroika and glasnost' domestically and within Eastern Europe

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a main idea that Source A and Source B share?

options.text: Both reject the idea that only one religious community can be saved by God.
options.label: key
options.why: Voltaire mocks the belief that 'my ant-hill is alone cherished by God,' and Rousseau would drive from the state anyone who says 'Outside the Church is no salvation.' Both attack religious exclusivity, a common Enlightenment theme.

options.text: Both argue that a single established national church is necessary to preserve the political loyalty of subjects.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rousseau states there 'can be no longer an exclusive national religion,' and Voltaire calls all people brethren. Neither defends one established church.

options.text: Both rest their case for tolerance chiefly on Scripture and the rulings of early church councils.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt cites Scripture or councils. Voltaire appeals to a common Creator and to reason, and Rousseau appeals to the duties of citizenship.

options.text: Source A ties toleration to the duties of citizenship, while Source B grounds it in shared human kinship.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This reverses the two authors. Rousseau ties tolerance to the duties of citizenship, and Voltaire grounds it in the kinship of all people as children of one Creator.

facts: Voltaire published the Treatise on Toleration in 1763.
Rousseau published The Social Contract in 1762.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Voltaire ridicules the 'ant-hill' that claims God's exclusive favor, and Rousseau condemns the dogma 'Outside the Church is no salvation.'
design.evidence_quote: But whoever dares to say: Outside the Church is no salvation, ought to be driven from the State

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historical context in which Voltaire wrote Source A after the execution of Jean Calas?

options.text: Protestants in France had lacked legal toleration since Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes.
options.label: key
options.why: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685, and French Protestants had no legal toleration until 1787. The 1762 execution of the Protestant Jean Calas in Toulouse took place in this setting of official discrimination.

options.text: The French Revolution had just dissolved the monasteries and required clergy to swear an oath to the constitution.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Civil Constitution of the Clergy and the clerical oath date from 1790, almost three decades after Voltaire wrote.

options.text: The Council of Trent had recently ordered the Catholic clergy to suppress Calvinist congregations throughout France.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563, two centuries before the Calas affair.

options.text: The Peace of Westphalia had just extended the principle of cuius regio eius religio to cover Calvinists in France.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1648 Peace of Westphalia recognized Calvinism within the Holy Roman Empire, not France, and it came more than a century before 1763.

facts: Louis XIV revoked the Edict of Nantes in 1685.
Jean Calas, a Protestant, was executed in Toulouse in 1762.
The Edict of Versailles of 1787 gave French Protestants civil status.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Voltaire wrote after the execution of Jean Calas, a Protestant, in Toulouse. That event reflects the legal position of Protestants in France after 1685.
design.evidence_quote: It does not require any great art or studied elocution to prove that Christians ought to tolerate one another.

items.stem: The approach to religion in Source B, which tolerates faiths whose dogmas respect the duties of citizenship, most directly anticipated which later development?

options.text: A 1789 French guarantee that religious opinions not disturbing public order be protected
options.label: key
options.why: Article 10 of the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen protected religious opinions as long as expressing them did not disturb public order. This echoes Rousseau's limit tied to citizenship.

options.text: The Congress of Vienna's restoration of legitimate monarchs and their established churches across Europe after 1815
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Vienna settlement restored legitimacy and alliances between throne and altar. It reflects conservatism, not Rousseau's civic toleration.

options.text: The ultramontane revival culminating in the First Vatican Council's 1870 declaration of papal infallibility
options.label: reversal
options.why: Ultramontanism strengthened papal authority over doctrine, which runs against Rousseau's subordination of dogma to civic duty.

options.text: The Pietist and Methodist revivals stressing personal conversion and emotional devotion within Protestant churches
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: These movements focused on inner piety and did not concern the state's rules for tolerating religions. Most of this activity also came before or alongside Rousseau, not after him.

facts: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789), Article 10, protected religious opinions provided their expression did not disturb public order.
The First Vatican Council declared papal infallibility in 1870.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Rousseau offers tolerance to religions 'so long as their dogmas contain nothing contrary to the duties of citizenship,' and the Declaration of 1789 later set a similar public-order limit.
design.evidence_quote: so long as their dogmas contain nothing contrary to the duties of citizenship

items.stem: Voltaire's image of 'nine hundred millions of us little insects' and a single favored 'ant-hill' in Source A was most likely intended to

options.text: mock religious exclusiveness by stressing how small any single faith is among humanity
options.label: key
options.why: The satire shrinks one sect's claim to God's favor down to an ant-hill among millions of people. The image shows how absurd it is to condemn 'all the rest' to eternal misery, a typical Voltairean use of irony against intolerance.

options.text: defend the Catholic Church's claim to be the only guardian of saving truth among all the world's peoples
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage ridicules, rather than defends, the claim that one community alone is 'cherished by God.'

options.text: urge naturalists to apply Newtonian methods of observation to the study of insects and other small creatures
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The insects are a metaphor for humankind. Nothing in the excerpt concerns natural history or scientific method.

options.text: warn that rapid population growth in Europe would exhaust food supplies unless trade with Asia expanded
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The population figure serves the argument about religious exclusivity, not economics. The excerpt says nothing about food supply or trade.

facts: Voltaire was known for using satire and irony against religious intolerance, as in his campaign over the Calas case in the 1760s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 'ant-hill' that claims to be 'alone cherished by God' while 'all the rest' are 'eternally wretched' is an ironic exaggeration of exclusive salvation.
design.evidence_quote: my ant-hill is alone cherished by God, who holds all the rest in horror and detestation

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Rousseau's claim about religious toleration in Source B?

options.text: It should be extended to faiths that tolerate others and respect civic duties.
options.label: key
options.why: Rousseau sets two conditions: religions must 'tolerate others,' and their dogmas must contain nothing 'contrary to the duties of citizenship.'

options.text: It should be granted to every religion without condition, including those that condemn other faiths as damned.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Rousseau says anyone claiming 'Outside the Church is no salvation' should be driven from the state, so his tolerance is conditional.

options.text: It should be determined by the papacy, since the prince must defer to the pope on all questions of doctrine.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Rousseau places civic duty above church dogma. He mentions the prince as pontiff only to describe theocracy, which he rejects outside theocratic states.

options.text: It should be withheld from all religions, since the state ought to abolish organized worship and promote atheism.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Rousseau says tolerance 'should be given to all religions that tolerate others.' He does not call for abolishing worship.

facts: Rousseau's chapter on civil religion in The Social Contract (1762) was among the passages condemned by authorities in Paris and Geneva.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Rousseau limits tolerance to religions that 'tolerate others' and whose dogmas do not conflict with 'the duties of citizenship.'
