design.evidence_quote: tolerance should be given to all religions that tolerate others

items.stem: Which of the following best explains the purpose of the excerpt from Thomas More's Utopia, published in 1516?

options.text: To condemn, through a fictional speaker, landowners who put wool profits ahead of rural families
options.label: key
options.why: The traveler attacks nobles, gentry and abbots who enclose land for sheep and turn families out. Using an invented speaker in a dialogue was a common way for Northern humanists to criticize the powerful.

options.text: To defend enclosure as a reform that raised farm output and helped England compete in the European cloth trade
options.label: reversal
options.why: The passage condemns enclosure as destroying houses and towns. It does not defend it.

options.text: To urge the crown to seize the lands of abbots and monasteries and sell them to loyal gentry families
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The passage mocks greedy abbots but proposes no confiscation. The dissolution of the monasteries came later, in 1536 to 1541.

options.text: To call for Protestant reform of church doctrine by exposing the greed and worldliness of the clergy
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The book appeared before Luther's protest of 1517, and More later opposed Protestantism. The criticism here is about land use, not doctrine.

facts: Thomas More published Utopia in Latin in 1516.
More was a Christian humanist and a friend of Erasmus who later wrote against Luther.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the passage is spoken by a traveler in the story, and the text attacks landowners who enclose land for sheep.
design.evidence_quote: the nobility and gentry, and even those holy men, the abbots! not contented with the old rents

items.stem: The speaker in the excerpt makes which of the following claims about rural England?

options.text: Converting farmland to sheep pasture was driving rural families off the land
options.label: key
options.why: The speaker says landowners enclose grounds for sheep and that owners and tenants are turned out and forced to move.

options.text: Royal forests and hunting parks, rather than private landowners, caused most of the decline of English villages
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Forests and parks are mentioned only sarcastically. The speaker blames enclosing landowners.

options.text: Abbots and other churchmen were the only landowners who resisted enclosing their estates for sheep pasture
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker names abbots among the people who enclose land.

options.text: Tenants willingly sold their farms to wool merchants because grazing paid better than growing grain
options.label: reversal
options.why: The speaker says tenants were removed by trick or force, or worn down until they had to sell.

facts: Enclosure in Tudor England often turned arable land into sheep pasture.
In Utopia, Raphael Hythloday blames enclosure for depopulating the countryside.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The speaker describes owners and tenants being turned out so that ground can be enclosed for sheep.
design.evidence_quote: the owners, as well as tenants, are turned out of their possessions by trick or by main force

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the early 1500s most directly contributed to the situation the speaker describes?

options.text: Growing demand for wool to supply the expanding cloth trade with the Low Countries
options.label: key
options.why: Profits from wool and cloth exports, especially through Antwerp, pushed landowners to turn fields into sheep pasture. That is the trend the speaker condemns.

options.text: The flood of American silver into Europe that drove the price revolution of the later sixteenth century
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Large silver inflows and the price revolution came mainly after the 1540s, decades after this 1516 text.

options.text: The dissolution of the monasteries, which transferred church estates to the crown and to lay buyers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The dissolution took place in 1536 to 1541. In the text, abbots still hold land.

options.text: The Portuguese spice trade around Africa, which shifted European commerce away from Mediterranean ports
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Portuguese route to Asia was real, but it had nothing to do with English landowners turning land over to sheep.

facts: In the early sixteenth century, English wool and woolen cloth were major exports, sold largely through Antwerp.
Henry VIII dissolved the monasteries between 1536 and 1541.
The price revolution driven by American silver was mainly a later sixteenth-century development.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The speaker says enclosure happens wherever sheep yield a softer and richer wool, which points to the market for wool.
design.evidence_quote: wherever it is found that the sheep of any soil yield a softer and richer wool than ordinary

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most limits the use of the excerpt as direct evidence of Thomas More's own views on enclosure?

options.text: The criticism is voiced by a fictional traveler in a literary dialogue
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says a traveler in the story speaks the passage. Because the book is a dialogue, its claims cannot simply be read as the author's own stated policy.

options.text: The book appeared after More had broken with Henry VIII over the king's break with the papacy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Utopia was published in 1516. More's conflict with Henry VIII came in the 1530s.

options.text: The book was printed in Latin, so ordinary English farmers who suffered from enclosure could not read it
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Latin text did limit who could read it, but that says nothing about whether the views are More's own.

options.text: More had no legal training and so could not have understood English property law or tenancy disputes
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context line says More was a lawyer.

facts: Utopia is written as a dialogue in which the traveler Raphael Hythloday speaks, and More appears as a character.
More's break with Henry VIII came in the 1530s; he was executed in 1535.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line states that the passage is spoken by a traveler in the story.

items.stem: EXTRA. Later in the sixteenth century, the English government responded to the kind of rural displacement described in the excerpt most directly by

options.text: passing vagrancy statutes and poor laws, culminating in the Poor Law of 1601
options.label: key
options.why: Families forced off the land added to the numbers of wandering poor. Tudor governments responded with vagrancy laws and parish poor relief, which ended in the Elizabethan Poor Law of 1601.

options.text: abolishing enclosure entirely and restoring open fields to the villages that had lost them
options.label: overstated
options.why: Tudor statutes tried to limit depopulating enclosure but never abolished it, and enclosure kept going.

options.text: binding peasants to the land as serfs, as landowners east of the Elbe were doing in the same period
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The second serfdom grew up in Eastern Europe. England did not reimpose serfdom.

options.text: sending the displaced rural poor to settle the first permanent English colonies in North America
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The first permanent English colony, Jamestown, was founded in 1607, after the sixteenth century, and it was a private venture rather than a resettlement program for the poor.

facts: The Elizabethan Poor Law was enacted in 1601.
Jamestown, the first permanent English colony in North America, was founded in 1607.
The second serfdom developed in Eastern Europe in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt ends with displaced families forced to leave and not knowing where to go. This is the growth in the wandering poor that later Tudor laws tried to deal with.
design.evidence_quote: are all forced to change their seats, not knowing whither to go

items.stem: The provisions in the excerpt most directly reflect which of the following developments in English government in the late seventeenth century?

options.text: The establishment of a constitutional monarchy in which the Crown needed Parliament's consent for key powers
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt makes suspending laws, levying money, and keeping a peacetime army illegal without Parliament's consent. These limits are central to the constitutional monarchy settled after the Glorious Revolution.

options.text: The strengthening of royal prerogative so that the monarch could rule and tax without summoning Parliament for years
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt calls taxation 'by pretence of prerogative' illegal, so this reverses its meaning.

options.text: The creation of a democratic system in which all adult men gained the right to vote for members of the House of Commons
options.label: overstated
options.why: The call for 'free' elections did not widen the franchise. Voting stayed limited to property holders long after 1689.

options.text: The abolition of the monarchy and House of Lords in favor of a republic governed by a Lord Protector and his army
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes the Interregnum of the 1650s. The 1689 document keeps the monarchy and is presented to William and Mary.

facts: The Bill of Rights of 1689 required parliamentary consent for taxation and for a standing army in peacetime.
The Glorious Revolution of 1688-1689 established a constitutional monarchy in England.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The repeated requirement of Parliament's consent for suspending laws, raising money, and keeping an army shows that the Crown's powers were now limited by Parliament.
design.evidence_quote: without consent of Parliament is illegal

items.stem: The first provision in the excerpt was most directly a response to which of the following?

options.text: James II's use of royal authority to suspend laws against Catholics and Protestant dissenters
options.label: key
options.why: James II's Declarations of Indulgence (1687 and 1688) set aside penal laws on his own authority. That is the 'suspending power' the excerpt declares illegal, and the context line ties the document to James's departure.

options.text: Louis XIV's revocation of the Edict of Nantes and the expulsion of Protestant pastors from France in 1685
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This really happened in 1685 and made English Protestants more anxious. But it was a French policy, and the clause is not addressing it.

options.text: The Scottish Covenanters' rebellion against an Anglican-style prayer book imposed by Charles I in 1637
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This crisis came half a century earlier and helped cause the Civil War. It had nothing to do with a royal power to suspend laws in 1689.

options.text: The Levellers' demands during the 1640s for a written constitution and the vote for most adult men
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Levellers were a radical movement of the Civil War era. The 1689 settlement did not respond to them, and it did not widen the vote.

facts: James II issued Declarations of Indulgence in 1687 and 1688 suspending penal laws against Catholics and dissenters.
James II fled England in December 1688 after William of Orange landed.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The clause condemning the 'pretended power of suspending the laws' by royal authority, together with the context line naming James II, points to James's suspension of the religious penal laws.
design.evidence_quote: the pretended power of suspending the laws or the execution of laws by regal authority

items.stem: The limits on royal power in the excerpt most clearly contrast with the government of Louis XIV of France, who

options.text: ruled without calling the Estates-General and raised revenue without its consent
options.label: key
options.why: The Estates-General did not meet between 1614 and 1789. Louis XIV taxed and kept a large army without any representative assembly's approval, which is the opposite of the excerpt's demand for Parliament's consent.

options.text: shared lawmaking authority with an elected assembly that voted each year on the size of the army
options.label: reversal
options.why: This describes the English model in the excerpt, not French absolutism under Louis XIV.

options.text: accepted a written charter drafted by the parlements guaranteeing their judges full freedom of debate
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The French parlements were law courts that Louis XIV restricted. He accepted no such charter, and freedom of debate is a right the excerpt gives the English Parliament.

options.text: abolished noble privileges and opened all royal offices to men of talent, as Napoleon's reforms later did
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Legal privilege was abolished in the Revolution and Napoleonic era. Louis XIV kept the society of orders in place.

facts: The French Estates-General did not meet between 1614 and 1789.
Louis XIV ruled personally from 1661 to 1715 and built a large standing army without the consent of a representative assembly.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt requires Parliament's grant for money and its consent for a peacetime army, which sets up the contrast with French rule without a representative body.
design.evidence_quote: without grant of Parliament

items.stem: The context in which the excerpt was presented to William of Orange and Mary suggests that Parliament intended to

options.text: set conditions on the new monarchs as they accepted the throne after James II's flight
options.label: key
options.why: Parliament presented the declaration to William and Mary after James left. This made the limits on royal power part of the terms of the new reign.

options.text: restore James II to power once he agreed to give up his Catholic faith and his standing army
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context line says the document went to William and Mary, not to James. Parliament treated the throne as vacant rather than seeking his return.

options.text: justify the execution of the king by declaring that the monarch was accountable to the people
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: A king was executed in 1649 (Charles I). In 1689 James II went into exile, and no king was executed.

options.text: announce that William and Mary would rule by divine right, independent of any parliamentary approval
options.label: reversal
options.why: The document ties royal actions to Parliament's consent, which contradicts any claim of rule independent of Parliament.

facts: In 1689 the Convention Parliament offered the crown jointly to William III and Mary II.
James II went into exile in France in 1688 and was not executed.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Parliament drew up the declaration and presented it to William and Mary after James II left, which shows it was meant to set terms for the new rulers.

items.stem: The principles about royal power in the excerpt are most consistent with the political ideas of

options.text: John Locke, who held that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed
options.label: key
options.why: Locke's Two Treatises of Government (published 1689) defended government limited by consent. This matches the excerpt's requirement that Parliament approve taxes and armies.

options.text: Thomas Hobbes, who held that subjects must yield to an undivided sovereign to escape a war of all against all
options.label: reversal
options.why: Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) argued for undivided sovereign power. That conflicts with the excerpt's division of power between Crown and Parliament.

options.text: Jacques-Benigne Bossuet, who claimed that kings answer only to God and hold authority from Him alone
options.label: reversal
options.why: Bossuet defended Louis XIV's divine-right absolutism, which the excerpt's limits on prerogative reject.

options.text: Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who argued that a general will of the people should guide a direct democracy
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Rousseau's Social Contract appeared in 1762, long after 1689. His idea of the general will is also quite different from a parliamentary check on a monarch.

facts: John Locke's Two Treatises of Government were published in 1689.
Thomas Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651.
Rousseau published The Social Contract in 1762.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's insistence that the Crown act only with Parliament's consent fits Locke's theory of government by consent.
design.evidence_quote: unless it be with consent of Parliament, is against law

items.stem: Which of the following claims about events in 1989 is made in the excerpt?

options.text: Poland's new government sought reforms like those envisioned in Hungary
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt says the Solidarity-led government intended many of the same political and economic reforms that Hungary's leaders and opposition groups envisaged.

options.text: Hungary's opposition groups rejected the reforms that the country's Communist leaders had proposed
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt groups Hungary's leaders and its opposition groups together as envisioning similar reforms, not as opposed.

options.text: Poland's June elections at once ended Communist rule in every member state of the Warsaw Pact
options.label: overstated
options.why: The excerpt says the elections eventually brought Solidarity to power in Poland and that other states began reforms later. It makes no claim of an immediate bloc-wide collapse.

options.text: East Germany, Bulgaria, and Czechoslovakia began reforming before Poland held its free elections
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt dates these reform efforts to late 1989, after Poland's June 1989 elections.

facts: Poland held partly free elections in June 1989, and Solidarity won nearly all the seats it was allowed to contest.
Tadeusz Mazowiecki of Solidarity became Polish prime minister in August 1989.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The second sentence links the reform goals of the Solidarity-led government in Poland to those of Hungary's leaders and opposition.
design.evidence_quote: intended to institute many of the same political and economic reforms in Poland that Hungary's leaders, as well as Hungary's opposition groups, envisaged

items.stem: Which of the following developments most directly contributed to the reform efforts in Warsaw Pact countries described in the excerpt?

options.text: Mikhail Gorbachev's policies of glasnost and perestroika in the Soviet Union
options.label: key
options.why: Gorbachev's openness and restructuring policies after 1985, together with his refusal to use force to hold the bloc together, gave Eastern European reformers room to act in 1989.

options.text: The Brezhnev Doctrine, which justified the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia in 1968
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Brezhnev Doctrine was used to suppress reform in the bloc. Moving away from it made 1989 possible, so it did not encourage reform.

options.text: The Maastricht Treaty, which turned the European Community into the European Union with a common currency plan
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Maastricht Treaty was signed in 1992, after the events described.

options.text: Marshall Plan aid that rebuilt the industries of Poland and Hungary after the Second World War
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Under Soviet pressure the Eastern bloc states turned down Marshall Plan aid, so it did not rebuild Poland or Hungary.

facts: Gorbachev became Soviet leader in 1985 and introduced glasnost and perestroika.
Under Soviet pressure, Poland and other Eastern bloc states declined Marshall Plan aid in 1947.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes a growing reform bloc within the Warsaw Pact in 1989, which requires knowing the Soviet policy changes that allowed it.
design.evidence_quote: the reform bloc within the Warsaw Pact was strengthened

items.stem: The reform efforts of 1989 described in the excerpt differed from the challenges to Communist rule in Hungary in 1956 and Czechoslovakia in 1968 in that the 1989 reforms

options.text: were not put down by Soviet military intervention
options.label: key
options.why: Soviet forces crushed the Hungarian uprising in 1956, and Warsaw Pact troops ended the Prague Spring in 1968. In 1989 Moscow did not intervene.

options.text: called for more political freedom and an end to strict censorship
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Demands for more freedom and less censorship were also central in 1956 and 1968, so they are a similarity, not a difference.

options.text: aimed to tighten central economic planning under direction from Moscow
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt describes political and economic reform away from the Soviet model, not tighter central planning.

options.text: were organized chiefly by NATO governments seeking to expand the Western alliance
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt credits domestic actors such as Solidarity and Hungary's leaders and opposition, not NATO governments.

facts: Soviet troops suppressed the Hungarian Revolution in 1956.
Warsaw Pact forces invaded Czechoslovakia in August 1968 and ended the Prague Spring.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes reform spreading through the Warsaw Pact in 1989 without any mention of suppression, which students compare with 1956 and 1968.
design.evidence_quote: Bulgaria, and Czechoslovakia began their own reform efforts

items.stem: Because the research for this study was completed in 1989, its usefulness to historians studying the end of the Cold War is limited mainly because its authors

options.text: could not know how the reform efforts would ultimately end
options.label: key
options.why: Writing while events were still happening, the authors described a reform bloc within the Warsaw Pact. They could not yet know that Communist rule and the alliance itself would soon collapse.

options.text: lacked any information about the results of Poland's June 1989 elections
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt reports that the June 1989 elections brought a Solidarity-led government to power, so the authors did know the results.

options.text: wrote mainly to justify Soviet policy to audiences inside the Warsaw Pact
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line says the study was written for the U.S. government, not for a Soviet-bloc audience.

options.text: were Solidarity activists who had taken part in the Polish negotiations
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or context identifies the authors as Solidarity participants. The study came from the Library of Congress.

facts: The Warsaw Pact was dissolved in 1991.
The Soviet Union dissolved in December 1991.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line notes that research was completed in 1989, and the excerpt still speaks of reform within the Warsaw Pact rather than its end.
design.evidence_quote: the reform bloc within the Warsaw Pact was strengthened

items.stem: Which of the following was a direct result of the developments described in the excerpt by the early 1990s?

options.text: The Warsaw Pact military alliance was formally dissolved
options.label: key
options.why: After Communist governments fell across Eastern Europe in 1989 and 1990, the Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved in 1991.

options.text: East German leaders built the Berlin Wall to halt mass emigration to the West
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 and came down in 1989. It was not a result of the 1989 reforms.

options.text: The Soviet Union annexed Poland and Hungary as new constituent socialist republics
options.label: reversal
options.why: Soviet control over Eastern Europe ended after 1989, and the USSR itself broke up in 1991.

options.text: Western powers founded NATO to defend against a Soviet attack on Western Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: NATO was founded in 1949, at the start of the Cold War.

facts: The Warsaw Pact was formally dissolved in 1991.
The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 and opened in November 1989.
NATO was founded in 1949.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt traces reform spreading among Warsaw Pact members in 1989, which led to the alliance's breakup.
design.evidence_quote: the German Democratic Republic (East Germany), Bulgaria, and Czechoslovakia began their own reform efforts

items.stem: Erasmus's description of believers who hold "a foolish but pleasant persuasion" about images of saints is best explained by which of the following?

options.text: A Christian humanist preference for inner piety grounded in scripture over reliance on outward rituals
options.label: key
options.why: Erasmus, a priest and humanist who stayed in the Church, mocked mechanical devotions (saluting a carved Barbara, candles for riches) because he valued an inward faith drawn from scripture and the early Church.

options.text: A Lutheran conviction that the papacy had no scriptural authority and that the Catholic Church must be abandoned
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Erasmus wrote in 1509, before Luther's protest, and never left the Catholic Church. The excerpt also does not attack papal authority.

options.text: A Calvinist belief that salvation was predetermined by God, which made prayers to saints for protection pointless
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Calvin's teaching on predestination came in the 1530s and later, and nothing in the excerpt refers to predestination.

options.text: A deist rejection of all revealed religion as superstition that rational inquiry would eventually replace
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Deism was an Enlightenment development. Erasmus was a priest who criticized abuses of Christian practice, not revealed religion as such.

facts: Erasmus wrote The Praise of Folly in 1509 and had it printed in 1511.
Erasmus remained a Catholic priest and urged a Christian piety based on study of scripture and the Church Fathers.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Folly calls trust in saints' images and set prayers a foolish persuasion, which reflects a humanist priest's dislike of devotion that is outward and mechanical.
design.evidence_quote: a foolish but pleasant persuasion

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim Folly makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Some clergy profit from popular devotions, and pardons give believers a false certainty about purgatory
options.label: key
options.why: Folly says these practices bring profit to mass priests and pardoners, and mocks people who trust counterfeit pardons and measure purgatory as if by an hourglass.

options.text: Images of saints such as Christopher and Barbara should be removed from churches and destroyed by magistrates
options.label: overstated
options.why: Folly ridicules what people believe about images, but the excerpt never calls for removing or destroying them. That was a later Protestant iconoclastic program.

options.text: Ordinary believers should read the Bible in their own languages instead of relying on Latin services led by priests
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Erasmus did elsewhere support wider reading of scripture, but this excerpt makes no claim about vernacular Bibles.

options.text: The pope alone is responsible for the sale of pardons and should be judged by a general council of the Church
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt blames mass priests and pardoners and the credulous people who buy pardons. It does not mention the pope or a council.

facts: Pardoners were clerics or agents who distributed indulgences, often in return for payments, in late medieval Europe.
Indulgences were understood to reduce the time a soul spent in purgatory.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Folly links devotions to clerical profit and mocks counterfeit pardons that claim to measure purgatory precisely.
design.evidence_quote: bring profit, especially to mass priests and pardoners

items.stem: The excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following broader developments?

options.text: Growing criticism of Church abuses before the Reformation, spread by humanists and the printing press
options.label: key
options.why: The work was printed in 1511 and widely read. It belongs to the pre-Reformation humanist critique of clerical greed and superstition, which print spread quickly.

options.text: Reforms of the Council of Trent, which ordered bishops to supervise preaching and condemned abuses in granting indulgences
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Trent met from 1545 to 1563, decades after this text was written in 1509.

options.text: The Scientific Revolution, whose mathematical methods led scholars to test religious claims through experiment
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The mention of a mathematical table is mockery, not scientific method. The Scientific Revolution developed mainly later in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

options.text: The French Wars of Religion, which led many Catholics to question devotion to saints and to their relics
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The French Wars of Religion began in 1562, long after Erasmus wrote this satire.

facts: Printing with movable type spread across Europe after Gutenberg's work around 1450.
The Praise of Folly was printed in 1511, six years before Luther's Ninety-Five Theses of 1517.
The Council of Trent met between 1545 and 1563.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates the writing to 1509 and the printing to 1511, which places the satire of pardoners in the period before the Reformation.
design.evidence_quote: hug themselves with their counterfeit pardons; that have measured purgatory by an hourglass

items.stem: Which of the following later developments most directly addressed concerns similar to those Folly raises about pardons and purgatory?

options.text: Martin Luther's objections in 1517 to the preaching of indulgences in the Holy Roman Empire
options.label: key
options.why: Luther's Ninety-Five Theses attacked the sale of indulgences and the false confidence it gave believers about purgatory, the same practice Folly satirizes.

options.text: Henry VIII's break with Rome in 1534, which was driven chiefly by his wish to annul his first marriage
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The English break with Rome was mainly about royal authority and the king's marriage, not about pardons or purgatory.

options.text: The Peace of Augsburg in 1555, which allowed each German prince to choose Lutheranism or Catholicism for his lands
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Augsburg was a political settlement of religious conflict, not a response to the selling of pardons.

options.text: The founding of the Jesuit order in 1540, which aimed to spread Catholic teaching through schools and missions
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Jesuits worked to strengthen Catholicism through education and missions. Their founding was not a protest against indulgence abuses.

facts: Martin Luther issued the Ninety-Five Theses against indulgence preaching in 1517.
The Society of Jesus received papal approval in 1540.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Folly's mockery of counterfeit pardons and precise measuring of purgatory anticipates Luther's 1517 attack on indulgences.
design.evidence_quote: hug themselves with their counterfeit pardons

items.stem: Which of the following most limits a historian's use of the excerpt as evidence of how common such devotional practices were in early sixteenth-century Europe?

options.text: As satire voiced by Folly, it exaggerates for effect and cannot show how common such practices were
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the speaker is a character named Folly. Satire exaggerates to make a point, so the text shows the author's criticism rather than reliable evidence of how widespread the practices were.

options.text: Because Erasmus was a Protestant reformer, he was hostile to every Catholic practice and ignored any positive aspects
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Erasmus was a Catholic priest and never became a Protestant.

options.text: Because it was written after the Council of Trent, it describes abuses that the Church had by then already corrected
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The text was written in 1509, decades before Trent opened in 1545.

options.text: Because it was printed only in an English translation, few continental readers in the sixteenth century could read it
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The credit line dates the English translation to 1668. The 1511 original was printed in Latin, which educated readers across Europe could read.

facts: The Praise of Folly was written in Latin and first printed in 1511.
The Council of Trent opened in 1545.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line identifies the speaker as the character Folly, which marks the excerpt as satire rather than a factual survey.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the main ideas of Source A and Source B?

options.text: Burke mourns lost aristocratic ideals, while Paine says Burke ignores the old order's victims.
options.label: key
options.why: Burke laments that loyalty to rank and dignified obedience are gone. Paine answers that Burke shows no compassion for those who suffered in the old regime's prisons, so he pities the plumage and forgets the dying bird.

options.text: Burke praises the revolution as a restoration of ancient liberties, while Paine warns that it will end in tyranny.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This reverses the two authors. Burke mourns the revolution's effects, and Paine defends the revolution against Burke.

options.text: Burke blames economic hardship for the revolution, while Paine credits Enlightenment philosophy for causing it.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Neither excerpt explains the revolution's causes in these terms. Burke mentions economists only to scorn the new age.

options.text: Burke defends absolute monarchy by divine right, while Paine defends a mixed constitution like Britain's.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Burke defended Britain's limited, inherited constitution, not divine-right absolutism. Paine attacked hereditary aristocracy and did not champion the British model.

facts: Edmund Burke published Reflections on the Revolution in France in 1790.
Thomas Paine published Rights of Man, Part I, in 1791 as a reply to Burke.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Burke regrets the passing of loyalty to rank and obedience, and Paine criticizes his lack of compassion for prisoners of the old regime.
design.evidence_quote: He pities the plumage, but forgets the dying bird.

items.stem: Burke's praise of "proud submission" and "dignified obedience" in Source A most likely reflects his view that

options.text: inherited hierarchy and custom gave society stability that abstract reason could not supply
options.label: key
options.why: Burke contrasts the age of chivalry with an age of sophisters and calculators. This fits his conservative argument that inherited institutions and habits of deference hold a society together better than rationalist schemes.

options.text: legitimate government must rest on a general will expressed directly by the entire body of sovereign citizens
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is Rousseau's idea of popular sovereignty, which revolutionaries drew on and Burke rejected.

options.text: the French nobility deserved to lose its tax exemptions and seigneurial dues in August 1789
options.label: reversal
options.why: Burke's lament for loyalty to rank points the opposite way. He regretted the overthrow of aristocratic order.

options.text: Parliament should defer to the Crown in all matters of policy, as under the Stuarts
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Burke was a Whig who supported limits on royal power under the settlement after 1688. He did not want a return to Stuart-style royal dominance.

facts: Burke's Reflections (1790) defended inherited institutions and tradition against revolutionary rationalism.
The National Assembly's August 1789 decrees abolished feudal privileges in France.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Burke praises deference and obedience and sets them against the cold rationalism of sophisters, economists and calculators.
design.evidence_quote: That of sophisters, economists, and calculators has succeeded

items.stem: The views expressed in Source A most closely anticipated which of the following developments of 1814 to 1815?

options.text: Diplomats at Vienna restored dynasties on the principle of legitimacy
options.label: key
options.why: Burke's defense of inherited rank and loyalty foreshadows the conservative settlement at the Congress of Vienna, where the powers restored ruling families such as the Bourbons as legitimate monarchs.

options.text: Napoleon's Hundred Days return, which rallied soldiers and peasants against the restored Bourbon king
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Hundred Days did happen in 1815, but it was a challenge to the restored order, not an outgrowth of Burke's conservatism.

options.text: The Napoleonic Code's spread, which ended noble privileges and guaranteed legal equality for men
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Code put revolutionary legal equality into law, which runs against Burke's defense of rank. It was also issued in 1804, not 1814 to 1815.

options.text: Britain's 1807 ban on the slave trade throughout its empire
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This came in 1807, outside the years named in the stem, and it has no link to Burke's argument about chivalry and rank.

facts: The Congress of Vienna (1814-1815) restored the Bourbons and other dynasties under the principle of legitimacy.
Napoleon's Hundred Days took place in 1815.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Burke's longing for loyalty to rank and obedience to inherited authority matches the restoration of legitimate dynasties after Napoleon.
design.evidence_quote: that generous loyalty to rank and sex, that proud submission, that dignified obedience

items.stem: EXTRA: Paine's reference to "the most miserable of prisons" in Source B most likely alludes to which event of 1789?

options.text: The Parisian crowd's capture of the Bastille in July
options.label: key
options.why: The Bastille was the royal prison that stood for old-regime despotism, and Paris crowds stormed it on 14 July 1789. Paine accuses Burke of ignoring the people held in such prisons.

options.text: The September Massacres of prisoners held in Paris jails
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These killings happened in 1792, after Paine's 1791 book. They were also violence by revolutionaries, not the abuses of the old regime.

options.text: The Tennis Court Oath sworn by Third Estate deputies
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The oath was taken in June 1789, but it was a political pledge and had nothing to do with prisons.

options.text: The Great Fear's peasant attacks on noble chateaux and records
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Great Fear was rural unrest in the summer of 1789. It did not involve a prison.

facts: Parisian crowds stormed the Bastille on 14 July 1789.
The September Massacres occurred in 1792.
The Tennis Court Oath was taken on 20 June 1789.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Paine refers to people who lived without hope in miserable prisons, which points to the Bastille as the symbol of old-regime imprisonment.
design.evidence_quote: a life without hope in the most miserable of prisons

items.stem: EXTRA: A historian using Source B as evidence about prisons under the French old regime would need to consider that Paine

options.text: wrote a polemic meant to discredit Burke's sympathy for the monarchy
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says the book was a reply to Burke, and the excerpt attacks Burke personally. Paine had reason to stress the old regime's cruelty to win the argument, which limits the source as neutral evidence.

options.text: had been held in the Bastille himself for publishing radical pamphlets before 1789
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the source or its context says this, and Paine was never held in the Bastille.

options.text: was writing as an official spokesman for the National Assembly to foreign governments
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context line describes Paine as an independent writer replying to Burke, not as a French official.

options.text: wrote decades later, after the Terror had changed his opinion of the revolution
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Paine published in 1791, before the Terror of 1793 to 1794.

facts: Rights of Man, Part I, was published in 1791 as a reply to Burke.
The Reign of Terror took place in 1793-1794.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Paine wrote the book as a reply to Burke, and the excerpt's personal attack on Burke shows its polemical purpose.
design.evidence_quote: It is painful to behold a man employing his talents to corrupt himself.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the claim Luther makes in theses 42 through 46 of the excerpt?

options.text: Charity toward the needy does more spiritual good than buying pardons
options.label: key
options.why: Theses 43 and 44 say that giving to the poor is 'a better work than buying pardons' because 'love grows by works of love,' while pardons only free a person from penalty.

options.text: Christians are justified by faith alone, so good works and sacraments are useless for their salvation
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Luther did later stress justification by faith, but this excerpt praises works of mercy and never calls good works or sacraments useless.

options.text: The pope has no authority over purgatory and should be resisted by German princes and their subjects
options.label: overstated
options.why: Thesis 42 actually says what the pope 'does not intend,' which treats papal intent as sound. The excerpt calls on no one to resist the pope.

options.text: Buying pardons is itself a kind of almsgiving, since the money funds church buildings that serve the poor
options.label: reversal
options.why: Thesis 42 denies that buying pardons can be compared to works of mercy, and thesis 45 says neglecting the needy to buy pardons earns God's indignation.

facts: Luther wrote the Ninety-Five Theses in 1517 to dispute the practice of indulgences.
An indulgence was understood to remit temporal punishment for sin, including in purgatory.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Theses 43-44 rank giving to the poor above buying pardons and explain that works of love make a person better.
design.evidence_quote: he who gives to the poor or lends to the needy does a better work than buying pardons

items.stem: Luther's criticism of preachers who promised that a coin in the money-box frees a soul (theses 27-28) was most directly a response to which of the following?

options.text: A papal indulgence campaign to raise money for rebuilding St. Peter's in Rome
options.label: key
options.why: In 1517 preachers such as Johann Tetzel were selling an indulgence proclaimed under Pope Leo X to fund St. Peter's Basilica. This is the money-box preaching that theses 27-28 attack.

options.text: The Council of Trent's decrees reaffirming indulgences and the doctrine of purgatory for Catholics
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563, decades after the theses of 1517.

options.text: Henry VIII's dissolution of English monasteries and his sale of their lands to the gentry
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The dissolution happened in the late 1530s, in England, and had nothing to do with indulgence preaching in Germany in 1517.

options.text: The Peace of Augsburg's grant to German princes of the right to choose their territory's faith
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Peace of Augsburg came in 1555, as a result of the religious conflict that Luther's challenge started.

facts: In 1517 Johann Tetzel preached an indulgence in German lands to raise funds for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica in Rome, under Pope Leo X.
The Peace of Augsburg was concluded in 1555.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Theses 27-28 attack preachers who tie the release of souls from purgatory to coins dropped in the money-box, which points to a fundraising indulgence campaign.
design.evidence_quote: so soon as the penny jingles into the money-box, the soul flies out [of purgatory]

items.stem: Criticisms like those in the excerpt most directly influenced which later response by the Catholic Church at its general council held between 1545 and 1563?

options.text: Trent's decrees curbing financial abuses in the granting of indulgences
options.label: key
options.why: The Council of Trent kept the doctrine of indulgences but condemned the evil gains connected with them and abolished the office of indulgence collectors. This responded to the kind of abuse that theses 27-28 describe.

options.text: Declaring that general church councils hold authority superior to that of the pope himself
options.label: reversal
options.why: Conciliarism belongs to the era of the Council of Constance (1414-1418). Trent ended by strengthening papal authority.

options.text: Requiring that the Mass and the Bible be offered in vernacular languages instead of Latin
options.label: reversal
options.why: Trent reaffirmed the Latin Vulgate as the authoritative Bible and kept the Latin Mass.

options.text: Allowing parish priests to marry so as to answer Protestant attacks on clerical immorality
options.label: reversal
options.why: Trent upheld clerical celibacy and rejected the Protestant acceptance of married clergy.

facts: The Council of Trent met in sessions between 1545 and 1563.
In 1562 Trent abolished the office of indulgence collectors, and its 1563 decree on indulgences upheld the doctrine while condemning the abuses and evil gains tied to it.
Trent reaffirmed clerical celibacy and the authority of the Latin Vulgate.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Thesis 28 links the money-box to 'gain and avarice,' the same financial abuse that Trent later moved to stop.
design.evidence_quote: gain and avarice can be increased

items.stem: Based on the context provided with the excerpt, Luther's original intended audience for the theses was most likely

options.text: Learned clergy and university scholars able to debate in Latin
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says Luther was a professor of theology and wrote the theses as propositions in Latin for debate, which was the format of an academic disputation.

options.text: German peasants who would hear the propositions read aloud in village churches
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The theses were later translated and spread to a wide public, but Luther wrote them in Latin, which most peasants could not read or understand.

options.text: Emperor Charles V and the princes assembled at the imperial Diet of Worms
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Luther did not appear before the Diet of Worms until 1521, four years after the theses.

options.text: Townspeople and merchants who funded hospitals and poor relief in Saxon cities
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The theses mention giving to the poor, but the Latin academic format shows they were not addressed to lay donors.

facts: The Ninety-Five Theses were written in Latin in 1517 as propositions for academic disputation.
Luther appeared before the Diet of Worms in 1521.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Luther was a theology professor who wrote the propositions in Latin for debate.

items.stem: The rapid spread of ideas like those in the excerpt across the German states in the years after 1517 was most directly made possible by

options.text: Printing presses that produced cheap copies and pamphlets
options.label: key
options.why: Movable-type printing, in use since the mid-fifteenth century, let printers quickly reproduce the theses and Luther's later German pamphlets for a wide readership.

options.text: Humanist schools that had taught most German peasants to read classical Latin
options.label: overstated
options.why: Humanist schooling reached a small educated elite. Most peasants were illiterate and could not read Latin.

options.text: Jesuit colleges that trained preachers to carry reform ideas across central Europe
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Jesuits were founded in 1540 and worked against Protestant ideas rather than spreading Luther's critique.

options.text: Decrees of the Diet of Worms that ordered public readings of Luther's writings
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Edict of Worms of 1521 declared Luther an outlaw and banned his writings.

facts: Gutenberg's movable-type printing press came into use in the Holy Roman Empire around the 1450s.
The Edict of Worms (1521) outlawed Luther and prohibited his writings.
The Society of Jesus received papal approval in 1540.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt is a 1517 set of propositions whose ideas spread far beyond the debate hall, which ties the question to the printing context of the period.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a difference between the main ideas of Source A and Source B?

options.text: Source A pledges joint military action against a named rival, while Source B settles colonial claims.
options.label: key
options.why: Source A commits both empires to fight together with their whole war strength if Russia attacks. Source B contains no military pledge. It trades recognition of Britain's position in Egypt for recognition of France's role in Morocco.

options.text: Source A divides overseas spheres of influence between two empires, while Source B pledges the full war strength of both signatories against Russia.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This switches the two documents. The pledge of whole war strength against Russia is in Source A, and the colonial spheres are in Source B.

options.text: Source A is limited to a defensive pact against Russia, while Source B binds Britain and France to fight Germany together if either is attacked.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The public articles of Source B make no promise of military help and never name Germany. Anglo-French military cooperation came later and was informal.

options.text: Source A aims to restore the Concert of Europe through regular congresses, while Source B rejects any role for France in North Africa.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Source A says nothing about congresses. Source B actually recognizes France's right to keep order in Morocco and to provide assistance there.

facts: Germany and Austria-Hungary signed the Dual Alliance on October 7, 1879, as a defensive pact aimed mainly at Russia.
The Entente Cordiale of 1904 settled Anglo-French colonial disputes, including Egypt and Morocco, and was not a formal military alliance.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A's Article 1 commits both empires to war if Russia attacks, while Source B exchanges recognition of positions in Egypt and Morocco.
design.evidence_quote: bound to come to the assistance one of the other with the whole war strength of their Empires

items.stem: Which of the following historical situations most directly provides context for the agreement in Source A?

options.text: Austro-Russian rivalry in the Balkans after the Congress of Berlin in 1878
options.label: key
options.why: The Congress of Berlin revised Russia's gains from its war with the Ottoman Empire, and Austria-Hungary was allowed to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina. Russia resented the outcome. Bismarck then tied Germany to Austria-Hungary against a possible Russian attack, which is why Russia is named in Source A.

options.text: The Franco-Russian military alliance concluded in the 1890s against the Central European powers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Franco-Russian alliance came in 1894, after Source A was signed. It was partly a response to the alliance in Source A, not its cause.

options.text: Russia's defeat by Britain, France, and the Ottoman Empire in the Crimean War of the 1850s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Crimean War ended in 1856, more than two decades before the treaty. The more direct tensions came from the Balkan crisis of 1875 to 1878.

options.text: Bismarck's Kulturkampf against the Catholic Church inside the new German Empire
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Kulturkampf was a domestic struggle over church and state. It does not explain a defensive treaty aimed at Russia.

facts: The Congress of Berlin in 1878 revised the Treaty of San Stefano after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-1878.
Austria-Hungary received the right to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina at the Congress of Berlin (1878).

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source A names Russia as the expected attacker, and that points to the Russian resentment and Balkan rivalry that followed the 1878 settlement.
design.evidence_quote: one of the two Empires be attacked by Russia

items.stem: Taken together, the two sources best illustrate which pattern in European great power relations between 1879 and 1914?

options.text: The growth of alliances and alignments that divided the powers into rival blocs
options.label: key
options.why: The Dual Alliance became the core of the Triple Alliance. The Entente Cordiale, together with the Anglo-Russian agreement of 1907, formed the Triple Entente. These two camps were opposed in 1914.

options.text: The revival of Concert of Europe congresses that settled disputes through collective agreement of all powers
options.label: reversal
options.why: Both documents are agreements between just two powers, partly kept secret. They point away from collective settlement by all the powers, not toward it.

options.text: The cooperation of conservative monarchies to suppress liberal and nationalist revolutions across the continent
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes the Holy Alliance and the Metternich era after 1815. It does not fit a treaty with republican France in 1904.

options.text: The end of colonial competition among European powers once Africa had been fully partitioned
options.label: overstated
options.why: Source B settles one Anglo-French dispute, but colonial rivalry went on. For example, Germany challenged France in Morocco in 1905 and 1911.

facts: Italy joined Germany and Austria-Hungary in the Triple Alliance in 1882.
The Anglo-Russian Convention of 1907 completed the Triple Entente of Britain, France, and Russia.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Both sources are bilateral agreements between great powers, one military and one colonial, and both became building blocks of the two opposing blocs of 1914.

items.stem: The context line for Source B notes that the published declaration came with secret articles. This most limits using Source B as evidence of which of the following?

options.text: The full set of commitments Britain and France made to each other
options.label: key
options.why: The secret articles were left out of the published text, so the excerpt cannot show everything the two governments agreed to.

options.text: The British government's public position on the political status of Egypt in 1904
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The published text states Britain's public position on Egypt directly, so secrecy does not weaken the source on this point.

options.text: French claims to a special role in Morocco based on its long border with North African lands
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The public text itself gives France's claim and the border argument, so the secret articles do not limit this use.

options.text: The reactions of German officials to Anglo-French cooperation in North Africa after 1904
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The source cannot show German reactions, but that is because it is an Anglo-French document. It has nothing to do with the secret articles.

facts: The Entente Cordiale of April 8, 1904, included secret articles that were not made public at the time.
Britain had occupied Egypt since 1882.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the declaration was published together with secret articles, so the excerpt is not the complete agreement.

items.stem: Which of the following developments most directly contributed to the agreement described in Source B?

options.text: The Fashoda crisis of 1898 between Britain and France over the upper Nile
options.label: key
options.why: At Fashoda, British and French forces confronted each other over control of the Nile valley, and France backed down. Afterward both governments looked for a settlement of their colonial rivalries, including Egypt, which Source B addresses.

options.text: The Crimean War, in which Britain and France fought as allies against Russia in the 1850s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The wartime cooperation ended decades earlier. Later Anglo-French rivalry over Africa, not the memory of the Crimean War, drove the 1904 settlement.

options.text: The Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, which set rules for European claims to territory in Africa
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The conference set general rules for claiming African territory. It did not settle the specific Anglo-French disputes over Egypt and Morocco in Source B.

options.text: The Dreyfus Affair, which divided French society over the army, antisemitism, and the republic
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Dreyfus Affair was a domestic French controversy and did not shape the colonial bargain over Egypt and Morocco.

facts: The Fashoda crisis of 1898 brought Britain and France to the brink of conflict over the upper Nile, and France withdrew.
Britain occupied Egypt in 1882, causing lasting friction with France.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Source B's French promise not to obstruct Britain in Egypt settles the Nile valley rivalry that had peaked at Fashoda.
design.evidence_quote: will not obstruct the action of Great Britain in that country

items.stem: Darwin's claim that humans bear in their bodies the stamp of a lowly origin best expresses which of the following scientific ideas?

options.text: Humans descended from earlier animal forms through the same natural processes that shaped other species
options.label: key
options.why: In The Descent of Man (1871), Darwin applied the theory of descent with modification by natural selection, set out in On the Origin of Species (1859), to human beings. The passage says humans rose to their place rather than being placed there.

options.text: Nations and races compete in a struggle for survival in which the strongest peoples rightly dominate the weaker ones
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is Social Darwinism, which others drew from evolutionary theory. The passage is about human biology, not about competition between nations.

options.text: Traits are passed between generations as discrete units, according to ratios worked out in Mendel's pea-plant experiments
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Mendel's work was largely ignored until it was rediscovered around 1900. Darwin did not use it, and the passage says nothing about how traits are inherited.

options.text: Human knowledge should rest only on observed facts, with society studied as a positive science as Comte proposed
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Comte's positivism belongs to the same era, but it is a philosophy of knowledge. It does not explain the claim that the human body shows a lowly origin.

facts: Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859.
Darwin published The Descent of Man in 1871, applying evolutionary theory to human origins.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The closing line says the human body carries the mark of a lowly origin, and the opening says humans rose to the summit of the organic scale rather than being placed there.
design.evidence_quote: Man still bears in his bodily frame the indelible stamp of his lowly origin

items.stem: Darwin's statement that he is concerned only with the truth as far as reason permits most likely reflects which purpose?

options.text: To present human evolution as a conclusion drawn from evidence, not from religious or emotional preference
options.label: key
options.why: Darwin sets aside hopes and fears and says he has given the evidence as best he can. This presents his conclusion as a matter of reason and evidence at a time when human evolution was religiously controversial.

options.text: To urge governments to adopt policies regulating marriage and reproduction in order to improve the national population
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Eugenics programs were promoted later by others. The passage proposes no policy at all.

options.text: To reconcile his findings with the Genesis account by showing that humans were placed at the summit of creation by design
options.label: reversal
options.why: Darwin explicitly says humans rose to the summit 'instead of having been aboriginally placed there.' That rejects special creation.

options.text: To argue that European peoples had risen further than others and were therefore entitled to govern overseas colonies
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The passage talks about humankind as a whole and says nothing about colonies or about ranking peoples.

facts: Darwin's theory of human descent from earlier animals provoked strong religious objection in the 1860s and 1870s, for example in the 1860 Oxford debate between Huxley and Bishop Wilberforce.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin says the question is about truth and evidence, not hopes or fears.
design.evidence_quote: we are not here concerned with hopes or fears, only with the truth as far as our reason permits us to discover it

items.stem: The excerpt is best understood in the context of which broader development in nineteenth-century Europe?

options.text: Growing confidence that empirical science could explain questions once answered mainly by religious authority
options.label: key
options.why: Darwin's naturalistic account of human origins fits a broader nineteenth-century trend, which also included positivism and the new geology, of treating science as the authority on questions about nature and humanity.

options.text: The Counter-Reformation's effort, led by the Jesuits and the Inquisition, to keep scientific inquiry under Church supervision
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Counter-Reformation belongs to the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, not the 1870s. It also cuts against Darwin's independent naturalistic method.

options.text: Pope Pius IX's acceptance in the Syllabus of Errors of reconciling Catholic doctrine with modern progress and science
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Syllabus of Errors (1864) condemned the idea that the pope should reconcile himself with progress, liberalism, and modern civilization.

facts: Pius IX issued the Syllabus of Errors in 1864, condemning the idea that the pope should reconcile with progress and modern civilization.
Auguste Comte developed positivism in the mid-nineteenth century, arguing that knowledge should rest on scientific observation.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin rests his claims about human origins on reason and evidence, and he praises the intellect that has explained the solar system. Both reflect the growing authority of science.
design.evidence_quote: his god-like intellect which has penetrated into the movements and constitution of the solar system

items.stem: EXTRA. In the late nineteenth century, some European writers adapted evolutionary ideas like those in the excerpt most commonly in order to do which of the following?

options.text: To portray imperial expansion and racial hierarchies as natural outcomes of competition among peoples
options.label: key
options.why: Social Darwinists, drawing on Herbert Spencer's phrase 'survival of the fittest,' applied the idea of struggle to societies. They used it to justify the New Imperialism and racial ranking.

options.text: To defend the balance of power and restoration of legitimate monarchs agreed upon at the Congress of Vienna
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Vienna settlement of 1815 came long before evolutionary theory, and it rested on the principle of legitimacy, not on biology.

options.text: To argue that universal natural rights, as proclaimed in the Enlightenment, required equal treatment of all colonized peoples
options.label: reversal
options.why: Social Darwinist arguments were generally used to deny equality to colonized peoples, not to defend it.

options.text: To support the papacy's claim, proclaimed at the First Vatican Council, that the pope was infallible on doctrine
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Papal infallibility (1870) was a doctrine of the Church, not an application of evolutionary theory.

facts: Herbert Spencer coined the phrase 'survival of the fittest' in 1864.
Social Darwinist ideas were used to justify the New Imperialism in the late nineteenth century.
The First Vatican Council proclaimed papal infallibility in 1870.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Darwin's picture of humans rising up the organic scale through natural processes is the kind of evolutionary idea that Social Darwinists carried over to societies and races.
design.evidence_quote: having risen, though not through his own exertions, to the very summit of the organic scale

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following best describes the main claim of the excerpt?

options.text: Despite their exalted mental and moral powers, humans show physical signs of descent from lower forms
options.label: key
options.why: Darwin lists sympathy, benevolence, and intellect, then concludes that humans 'still' bear the stamp of a lowly origin. This was a central claim of his theory of human descent.

options.text: Humans' god-like intellect and sympathy prove that they were created separately from the rest of the animal world
options.label: reversal
options.why: Darwin praises these qualities but says they exist alongside the evidence of a lowly origin. He does not treat them as proof of separate creation.

options.text: Because human sympathy now reaches the humblest creatures, moral progress will soon end war and social conflict
options.label: overstated
options.why: Darwin notes how far human sympathy reaches, but he predicts nothing about ending war. He mentions only a hope for a higher destiny in the distant future.

options.text: Humans have reached a final, perfected condition at the summit of nature and can expect no further development
options.label: reversal
options.why: Darwin says humans may hope for 'a still higher destiny in the distant future,' so he does not describe a final, perfected condition.

facts: In The Descent of Man (1871), Darwin argued that humans share common ancestry with other animals.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The final sentence sets humanity's noble qualities against the lasting evidence of lowly origin in the human body.
design.evidence_quote: with all these exalted powers—Man still bears in his bodily frame the indelible stamp of his lowly origin

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the cartoonist's point of view about the River Thames in 1858?

options.text: The filthy river was breeding deadly diseases that threatened the city's people.
options.label: key
options.why: Father Thames presents ragged children labeled Diphtheria, Scrofula and Cholera to the worried crowned figure of London, so the polluted river is shown as the source of disease.

options.text: London's busy river and factories were signs of national progress that outweighed their costs to the city.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The factory chimneys sit behind a scene of filth and sickness. The cartoon criticizes these conditions and does not celebrate them.

options.text: Disease in London came mainly from immigrants arriving by ship, not from conditions in the river.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the image points to immigrants. The diseases are drawn as the river's own offspring.

options.text: The city's sickness was a punishment for sin that only religious revival among Londoners could cure.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The cartoon has no religious message about sin. It ties disease to the dirty water and suggests Parliament needs to act.

facts: In the summer of 1858 the stench of the polluted Thames, later called the Great Stink, became a major public problem in London.
Cholera epidemics struck London several times in the mid-nineteenth century, including 1848-1849 and 1853-1854.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The title and the labeled children (Diphtheria, Scrofula, Cholera) presented by the river figure to the personification of London show the cartoonist's view that the river spread disease.
design.evidence_quote: FATHER THAMES INTRODUCING HIS OFFSPRING TO THE FAIR CITY OF LONDON.

items.stem: The conditions shown in the cartoon are best understood in the context of which broader nineteenth-century development?

options.text: Rapid urban growth that outpaced cities' systems for removing sewage and waste
options.label: key
options.why: As industrialization drew people into cities, London's population grew quickly. Its waste ran into the Thames faster than the city's drainage could cope with, producing the filth and disease the cartoon shows.

options.text: The spread of plague from Asian trade routes that repeatedly emptied European port cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Repeated waves of plague belong to the late medieval and early modern centuries. They do not explain the problems of 1858.

options.text: The repeal of the Corn Laws, which lowered bread prices for workers in British manufacturing towns
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846, but that was a trade policy about grain. It does not explain why the river was polluted.

options.text: Enclosure of common lands, which ended most farming in England and left the countryside largely empty
options.label: overstated
options.why: Enclosure did push rural people toward towns, but it did not end farming or empty the countryside.

facts: Britain's urban population grew rapidly during industrialization, and by 1851 more Britons lived in towns than in the countryside.
In the mid-nineteenth century much of London's sewage drained into the Thames.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The factory chimneys, dense buildings and dirty river in the background tie the scene to an industrial city whose waste system had been overwhelmed.

items.stem: Which of the following best explains how the British state responded, in the decades after 1858, to conditions like those shown in the cartoon?

options.text: Public authorities took on new responsibility for building sewers and improving water supplies.
options.label: key
options.why: After the Great Stink, Parliament authorized the Metropolitan Board of Works to build Joseph Bazalgette's intercepting sewers. This was part of a wider growth of state involvement in public health.

options.text: Parliament left sanitation to private charities, holding that state spending on cities violated laissez-faire principles.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Parliament did the opposite. It paid for a large public sewer system and widened public health powers.

options.text: The Ten Hours Act limited the working day for women and young people in textile mills to ten hours.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 1847 Ten Hours Act was a real reform, but it dealt with factory labor, not with river pollution or sewage.

options.text: New sewer and water systems quickly wiped out cholera, diphtheria, and every other infectious disease in London.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The sewers sharply reduced cholera, but they did not end all infectious disease in London.

facts: In 1858 Parliament gave the Metropolitan Board of Works authority and funding to build a new main sewer system for London.
Engineer Joseph Bazalgette designed London's intercepting sewers, which were built in the 1860s and 1870s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The caption calls the cartoon a design for a fresco in the Houses of Parliament, which points to Parliament as the body expected to deal with the river.
design.evidence_quote: A Design for a Fresco in the New Houses of Parliament.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following was a similar response to urban conditions in another European country during the mid-nineteenth century?

options.text: Haussmann's rebuilding of Paris, which included new sewers and water supplies
options.label: key
options.why: Under Napoleon III, from the 1850s Baron Haussmann rebuilt Paris with wide boulevards, new sewers and better water supplies. Like London's sewers, this was a state answer to crowded, unhealthy cities.

options.text: Alexander II's emancipation of the serfs, which gave Russian peasants personal freedom and land obligations
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1861 emancipation was a rural social reform. It had nothing to do with urban sanitation.

options.text: Bismarck's sickness and accident insurance laws, which covered German industrial workers in the 1880s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These laws came in the 1880s, not the mid-century, and they insured workers rather than cleaning up city water or sewage.

options.text: The creation of the Zollverein, a customs union that removed tariffs among many German states
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Zollverein was an economic union about trade. It did not address urban health.

facts: Georges-Eugene Haussmann, prefect of the Seine under Napoleon III from 1853 to 1870, directed a rebuilding of Paris that included new sewers and water supply.
Alexander II emancipated the Russian serfs in 1861.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The cartoon's focus on a polluted city river and disease anchors a comparison with other states' rebuilding of urban sanitation.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following pieces of evidence from the period would most directly support the cartoon's suggestion that polluted water spread cholera?

options.text: John Snow's 1854 mapping of London cholera deaths around a contaminated public water pump
options.label: key
options.why: Snow's study of the Broad Street outbreak linked cholera cases to one contaminated water source. That backs the cartoon's link between dirty water and the child labeled Cholera.

options.text: Edward Jenner's experiments showing that inoculation with cowpox protected people against smallpox infection
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Jenner's work in the 1790s was about smallpox vaccination. It says nothing about water and cholera.

options.text: Joseph Lister's use of carbolic acid to reduce infections after surgery in Glasgow hospital wards
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Lister's antiseptic methods dealt with wound infection after surgery, not with waterborne disease.

options.text: Thomas Malthus's argument that population growth would outrun food supply and bring famine and disease
options.label: too_broad
options.why: Malthus wrote about population pressure in general and did not tie any particular disease to contaminated water.

facts: In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak in Soho, London, to the Broad Street water pump.
Edward Jenner demonstrated smallpox vaccination using cowpox in 1796.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The child labeled Cholera stands in the polluted river beside Father Thames, so the cartoon implies that the river water carried the disease.
design.evidence_quote: CHOLERA.

items.stem: Based on the excerpt, Bismarck's main claim in his 1862 speech was that

options.text: great political questions would be settled by military strength rather than by parliamentary debate
options.label: key
options.why: Bismarck says the great questions are decided not by speeches and majority votes but by blood and iron, meaning armed force.

options.text: Prussia should preserve the boundaries set at Vienna and cooperate with Austria inside the German Confederation
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says the Vienna boundaries were not favourable to Prussia, which is the opposite of defending them.

options.text: Prussia's liberal deputies should lead national unification through elected assemblies like the one at Frankfurt in 1848
options.label: reversal
options.why: Bismarck calls the reliance on speeches and votes in 1848 and 1849 a great blunder.

options.text: Prussia should widen the franchise so that popular majorities could legitimize a stronger and more unified state
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt calls for a wider franchise; Bismarck dismisses majority votes as the way to decide national questions.

facts: Bismarck gave his blood and iron speech to the budget committee of the Prussian Landtag in September 1862.
The Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 to 1849 did not manage to unify Germany.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The quoted line contrasts speeches and majority votes with blood and iron.
design.evidence_quote: not by speeches and majority votes are the great questions of the time decided

items.stem: Which of the following developments in the decade after 1862 would most directly support the argument Bismarck makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Prussian victories over Denmark, Austria, and France leading to the German Empire in 1871
options.label: key
options.why: Unification came through three wars between 1864 and 1871, which fits Bismarck's claim that blood and iron, not votes, would settle the German question.

options.text: The continued operation of the Zollverein, which tied the economies of most German states to Prussia through tariffs
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The customs union was real and helped Prussia, but economic integration does not show that military force settled the question.

options.text: The Kulturkampf, in which Bismarck's government passed laws restricting the Catholic Church's role in German education
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Kulturkampf was a domestic religious conflict after unification and has nothing to do with whether war or debate unified Germany.

options.text: The Prussian Landtag's success in forcing Bismarck to abandon army reform after the budget conflict of the early 1860s
options.label: reversal
