options.why: The Landtag did not force him to drop army reform. Bismarck went ahead with it, and the 1866 Indemnity Bill approved the spending after the fact.

facts: Prussia fought Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866, and France in 1870 to 1871.
The German Empire was proclaimed at Versailles in January 1871.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Bismarck argues that putting the most military power possible in the king's hands is the only way to carry out the national policy.
design.evidence_quote: it cannot be done with speeches and celebrations and songs, it can only be done by blood and iron

items.stem: The approach to national unification described in the excerpt was most similar to which of the following developments elsewhere in Europe in the mid-nineteenth century?

options.text: Cavour's use of diplomacy and war against Austria to expand Piedmont-Sardinia in Italy
options.label: key
options.why: Like Bismarck, Cavour followed a power-based Realpolitik. He allied with France and fought Austria in 1859 to enlarge a monarchical state.

options.text: Mazzini's Young Italy movement, which sought a unified Italian republic through popular uprisings and education
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Mazzini stood for romantic, popular republican nationalism, which is closer to the 1848 approach that Bismarck rejected.

options.text: British Chartists' mass petitions to Parliament demanding universal male suffrage and secret ballots
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Chartists relied on petitions and pressure on Parliament, the kind of method Bismarck dismissed.

options.text: The repeal of the Corn Laws in 1846 after a sustained campaign by the Anti-Corn Law League in Britain
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This was a change in British economic policy won by campaigning and votes, not national unification by force.

facts: Cavour, prime minister of Piedmont-Sardinia, allied with Napoleon III and fought Austria in 1859.
Mazzini founded Young Italy in 1831.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Bismarck says the Prussian state should build up its power and wait for the right moment to use it, which is Realpolitik led by the state.
design.evidence_quote: Prussia must concentrate its power and hold itself ready for the favourable moment

items.stem: Bismarck's 1862 speech described in the excerpt was given in which of the following historical situations?

options.text: A dispute between the Prussian king and liberal deputies over funding for army reform
options.label: key
options.why: Bismarck became minister-president in 1862 during the constitutional conflict over the army budget. That is why he spoke to the budget committee and appealed for confidence.

options.text: Prussia's defeat of Austria and its creation of the North German Confederation under Prussian leadership
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: These events came in 1866 and 1867, several years after the speech.

options.text: The revolutions that forced Frederick William IV to grant a constitution and summon a Prussian assembly
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The speech looks back on 1848 and 1849 as a blunder, so it was given well after those revolutions.

options.text: The conflict between Bismarck's government and the Catholic Church over schools and clerical appointments
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Kulturkampf began in the 1870s, after unification.

facts: Bismarck was appointed Prussian minister-president in September 1862 during a deadlock over army reform funding.
The liberal majority in the Prussian Landtag refused to approve the budget for the army reorganization.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Bismarck appeals for the deputies' trust and argues for giving the king military power, which points to the budget conflict with the legislature.
design.evidence_quote: He appealed for confidence: "Do not force a quarrel; we are honest people and you can trust us."

items.stem: Headlam's use of the explanation Bismarck gave in later years of what he really meant is significant to historians because that explanation

options.text: may reflect hindsight shaped by the success of unification after 1871
options.label: key
options.why: A later explanation may have been shaped by how things turned out, so it could change what the 1862 words meant at the time.

options.text: was recorded by Headlam himself while he sat in the Prussian budget committee in 1862
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Headlam was a British historian writing in 1899, and nothing suggests he was present in 1862.

options.text: shows that Bismarck rejected military force once the German Empire had been established
options.label: reversal
options.why: In the later explanation Bismarck repeats that only blood and iron could achieve the policy.

options.text: proves that British opinion in 1899 was united in condemning Prussian militarism
options.label: overstated
options.why: One historian's account cannot show what British opinion as a whole thought, and the excerpt condemns nothing.

facts: The German Empire was founded in 1871, almost three decades before Headlam published his book in 1899.
Bismarck left office in 1890 and lived until 1898.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Headlam says he is relying on Bismarck's own later account of what he meant, not only on the 1862 words.
design.evidence_quote: He has told us in later years what he really meant

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Mill makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Society may restrict an individual's freedom of action only to prevent harm to other people.
options.label: key
options.why: Mill states that the sole end warranting interference with liberty is self-protection, and that power may rightfully be used against a person's will only to prevent harm to others.

options.text: Governments should use legal penalties rather than public opinion to enforce shared moral standards on citizens.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mill treats both legal penalties and the moral coercion of public opinion as forms of compulsion that his principle limits. He does not want either one used to enforce moral conformity.

options.text: Individuals hold natural rights granted by God that no state may ever restrict under any circumstances whatsoever.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Mill does not ground his principle in divine natural rights. He also explicitly allows interference to prevent harm to others, so liberty is not unlimited.

options.text: A civilized community must use compulsion to improve individuals' moral character for their own good.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This is the opposite of Mill's claim. He limits compulsion to preventing harm to others and does not accept improving a person for his own good as a reason for it.

facts: John Stuart Mill published On Liberty in 1859.
On Liberty argues that the only legitimate reason for coercing an individual is to prevent harm to others (often called the harm principle).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says outright that power over a member of a civilised community is rightful only to prevent harm to others.
design.evidence_quote: the only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others

items.stem: Mill's argument about limiting the power of society over the individual is best understood in the context of which of the following nineteenth-century developments?

options.text: The spread of liberal ideas favoring limited government and protections for individual freedoms
options.label: key
options.why: In the nineteenth century, liberals called for constitutional limits on authority and for civil liberties. Mill's essay is a classic statement of that liberal tradition.

options.text: The efforts of enlightened absolutists such as Frederick the Great to reform their states from above by royal decree
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Enlightened absolutism belongs to the eighteenth century, and it relied on strong monarchical power rather than limiting it.

options.text: The rise of Marxist socialism, which called on workers to seize the state and abolish private ownership of property
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Marxism was a contemporary ideology, but it focused on class struggle and collective ownership, not on shielding individuals from social coercion.

options.text: The Romantic movement's turn toward emotion, nature, and national folk traditions as sources of artistic inspiration
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Romanticism was a real cultural movement, but it does not explain a political argument about the limits of legal and social compulsion.

facts: Nineteenth-century liberalism advocated constitutional government, limits on state power, and civil liberties.
Frederick the Great ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt sets strict limits on the compulsion and control that society may exercise over the individual, which is a core concern of nineteenth-century liberalism.
design.evidence_quote: to govern absolutely the dealings of society with the individual in the way of compulsion and control

items.stem: The principle stated in the excerpt is most similar to ideas expressed in which earlier development?

options.text: The 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man, which defined liberty as the freedom to do anything that harms no one else
options.label: key
options.why: The 1789 French declaration defined liberty as the freedom to do whatever does not injure others. Seventy years later, Mill makes harm to others the only limit on individual liberty.

options.text: The Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, which Metternich used to censor the press and monitor universities across the German Confederation
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Carlsbad Decrees imposed state control over speech and education. That is the kind of coercion Mill's principle rejects.

options.text: Robert Owen's New Lanark experiment, which sought to reshape workers' character through a carefully planned community and schooling
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Owen's utopian socialist project aimed to shape character collectively. It was not an argument for limiting society's power over individuals.

options.text: The Congress of Vienna settlement of 1815, which restored legitimate monarchs and set up a balance of power among the great powers
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Vienna settlement dealt with conservative restoration and international order, not with the limits of coercion over individuals.

facts: The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (1789) defines liberty as the power to do whatever does not injure others.
The Carlsbad Decrees (1819) imposed censorship and university surveillance in the German Confederation.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Mill's claim that preventing harm to others is the only legitimate reason to restrain someone parallels the 1789 definition of liberty.
design.evidence_quote: the sole end for which mankind are warranted, individually or collectively, in interfering with the liberty of action of any of their number, is self-protection

items.stem: Which of the following best explains why Mill included the moral coercion of public opinion, not only legal penalties, in the principle described in the excerpt?

options.text: He feared that in societies moving toward popular rule, majority opinion could suppress individual dissent.
options.label: key
options.why: Mill names public opinion as a form of coercion alongside the law. This reflects a liberal worry that as political participation widened, majorities could pressure nonconforming individuals.

options.text: He believed the Catholic Church still controlled British censorship laws and wanted Parliament to abolish its church courts.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt mentions the Catholic Church. The claim is also historically inaccurate for nineteenth-century Britain.

options.text: He wanted to persuade workers that trade unions should use public shaming rather than strikes to win higher wages.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt does not discuss labor organizing. Mill also treats public pressure as a form of coercion to be limited, not as a tactic to recommend.

options.text: He argued that public opinion was a harmless force that should replace legal penalties as the main tool of social control.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mill puts public opinion in the same category as legal force: a means of compulsion that his principle restricts.

facts: Nineteenth-century liberals such as Mill worried about the tyranny of the majority as political participation expanded.
Britain's Reform Act of 1832 expanded the electorate.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Mill explicitly lists public opinion alongside legal penalties as means of compulsion that his principle governs.
design.evidence_quote: or the moral coercion of public opinion

items.stem: The principle in the excerpt is most consistent with which cause Mill later championed as a member of the British Parliament?

options.text: Voting rights for women, which he proposed in Parliament during debate over the Second Reform Act of 1867
options.label: key
options.why: During the 1867 Reform Act debate, Mill moved an amendment to give women the vote. This extended his liberal commitment to individual liberty and equal standing.

options.text: Restoring protective tariffs on imported grain, which Parliament had repealed in 1846 under pressure from the Anti-Corn Law League
options.label: reversal
options.why: Mill was a liberal political economist who supported free trade, not a return to the Corn Laws.

options.text: Expanding the British Empire in Africa through the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885, which divided the continent among European powers
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Mill died in 1873, more than a decade before the Berlin Conference.

options.text: Laws compelling attendance at the established Church of England to promote religious uniformity among British subjects
options.label: reversal
options.why: Forcing church attendance would be coercion of conduct that harms no one else, which Mill's principle forbids.

facts: Mill served as a member of Parliament from 1865 to 1868 and proposed women's suffrage during debate on the Reform Act of 1867.
The Corn Laws were repealed in 1846.
The Berlin Conference met in 1884 to 1885.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's limit on power over any member of a civilised community fits Mill's later push to extend political rights to women. The context line identifies Mill as an English thinker writing in 1859.
design.evidence_quote: power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilised community, against his will

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main claim Rousseau makes about the social compact in the excerpt?

options.text: Joining the compact turns separate individuals into one collective body with a shared will
options.label: key
options.why: Rousseau says the act of association replaces each contracting party's individual personality with a moral and collective body that has its own unity and will.

options.text: A ruler receives absolute power from the people, who then surrender any right to resist him
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is closer to Hobbes's Leviathan (1651). Rousseau places members under the general will of the whole body, not under one ruler.

options.text: Each person keeps natural rights to life, liberty, and property that no government may override
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This is Locke's position. Rousseau says each person puts his person and all his power in common, so individuals do not hold back separate rights against the whole.

options.text: Society functions best when private interests compete freely and the state stays out of the economy
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: This resembles Adam Smith's economic thought. The excerpt is about forming a political body, not about markets.

facts: Rousseau's The Social Contract was published in 1762.
Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) argued that subjects should give up power to an absolute sovereign.
Locke's Two Treatises of Government (1689) defended natural rights to life, liberty, and property.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt says the compact replaces individual personalities with a collective body that has a single will.
design.evidence_quote: this act of association creates a moral and collective body

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the historical situation in which Rousseau published the argument in the excerpt?

options.text: French kings claimed to rule by divine right, answerable to God rather than to their subjects
options.label: key
options.why: In 1762 Louis XV ruled France as an absolute monarch who claimed divine right. Rousseau's claim that the supreme direction belongs to the general will of the associated people challenged that idea of sovereignty.

options.text: French revolutionary assemblies were drafting written constitutions grounded in the sovereignty of the nation
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: French revolutionary constitution-making began in 1789, about three decades after the book appeared.

options.text: English Parliament had recently deposed James II and passed a Bill of Rights limiting the crown
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Glorious Revolution and the Bill of Rights happened in 1688 and 1689, more than seventy years before 1762.

options.text: Napoleon's armies were imposing a uniform civil code and ending feudal privileges across Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Napoleonic Code dates from 1804, decades after the excerpt was written.

facts: Louis XV reigned in France from 1715 to 1774.
The French Revolution began in 1789.
The Napoleonic Code was issued in 1804.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates the book to 1762 and says Rousseau lived mostly in France, a kingdom then ruled by an absolute monarch.
design.evidence_quote: under the supreme direction of the general will

items.stem: Rousseau's idea of the general will, as expressed in the excerpt, most directly influenced which of the following later developments?

options.text: Jacobins in the 1790s invoked the will of the people to justify radical revolutionary policies
options.label: key
options.why: Robespierre and other Jacobins openly admired Rousseau. They used ideas of popular sovereignty and the general will to justify revolutionary government.

options.text: Diplomats at the Congress of Vienna restored legitimate dynasties to their thrones across Europe after 1815
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Vienna settlement rested on dynastic legitimacy, which rejected the idea that sovereignty comes from a collective body of citizens.

options.text: French Physiocrats urged rulers to abolish internal tariffs and allow free trade in grain and land
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Physiocrats worked in the same period, but their arguments about economic freedom did not grow out of Rousseau's theory of the general will.

options.text: Frederick II of Prussia introduced religious toleration and legal reform while keeping full royal power
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Frederick's enlightened absolutism kept sovereignty in the monarch's hands, so it does not reflect sovereignty of the general will.

facts: The Jacobins under Robespierre dominated the French revolutionary government in 1793 and 1794.
The Congress of Vienna (1814 to 1815) restored legitimate monarchies.
Frederick II ruled Prussia from 1740 to 1786.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt places supreme authority in the general will of an assembly of members, an idea later taken up by French revolutionaries.
design.evidence_quote: composed of as many members as the assembly contains votes

items.stem: The excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following broader intellectual trends of the eighteenth century?

options.text: Philosophes grounding political authority in reason and consent rather than tradition
options.label: key
options.why: Rousseau explains political authority as coming from a voluntary compact among individuals, which fits the Enlightenment effort to justify government by reason and consent.

options.text: Protestant reformers rejecting papal authority and arguing for salvation by faith alone
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Reformation belongs to the sixteenth century and dealt with religious doctrine, not with social contract theory.

options.text: Mercantilist states seeking to increase national wealth through colonies, tariffs, and export surpluses
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Mercantilism was an economic policy of the period. It does not explain a philosophical argument about where sovereignty comes from.

options.text: Romantic writers celebrating national folk traditions and emotion in reaction against industrial cities
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Romanticism developed mainly in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, and the excerpt is a rational analysis of a contract, not a celebration of folk tradition.

facts: The Enlightenment flourished in eighteenth-century Europe.
The Protestant Reformation began in 1517.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Rousseau reduces the social compact to its essential terms, which shows him deriving political authority from a rational agreement.
design.evidence_quote: If then we discard from the social compact what is not of its essence

items.stem: Which of the following most limits the usefulness of the excerpt as evidence of how eighteenth-century European governments actually operated?

options.text: It describes an ideal theoretical association, not the practice of any existing state
options.label: key
options.why: Rousseau sets out the essential terms of a hypothetical compact. That is political theory, not a description of how actual governments of the time worked.

options.text: It was written after the French Revolution and reflects disillusionment with revolutionary violence
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The book was published in 1762, before the Revolution began in 1789.

options.text: It was commissioned by the French crown and so presents royal policies in a favorable light
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the source suggests the crown commissioned it. In fact, the book was banned in Paris.

options.text: It records debates in the Genevan assembly and so reflects only the views of local magistrates
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt is one author's philosophical argument, not a record of any assembly's debates.

facts: The Social Contract was published in 1762.
The Social Contract was banned in Paris and Geneva soon after it was published.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The text discusses the essential terms of an abstract compact rather than describing any specific government.
design.evidence_quote: we shall find that it reduces itself to the following terms

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Acton's claim about how relations between states were understood at the time of the seizure of Silesia?

options.text: Statesmen of the period widely accepted that acts done for the state were not judged like private crimes.
options.label: key
options.why: Acton says states 'acknowledged no law over them' and that serious men would admit that what is done for the state differs from what an individual may do.

options.text: Frederick's invasion was condemned in 1740 as a clear breach of a widely accepted European code of international law.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton states that 'No accepted code regulated the relations between States,' the opposite of this claim.

options.text: Frederick invaded Silesia chiefly to protect its Protestant population from religious persecution by Catholic Habsburg officials.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt names territorial claims, the succession, Russia, and ambition; it says nothing about religion.

options.text: Frederick's personal ambition by itself explains the seizure, since outside circumstances offered him no particular opportunity.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Acton mentions ambition but also points to the disputed succession and the Russian empress's death as favorable circumstances.

facts: Frederick II of Prussia invaded the Habsburg province of Silesia in December 1740.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton's description of states as acknowledging no higher law and of actions in the public interest being judged differently.
design.evidence_quote: States were absolute, and acknowledged no law over them.

items.stem: The excerpt's reference to a succession that "was about to be disputed" is best explained by which of the following?

options.text: The death of Charles VI left Maria Theresa as heir under the Pragmatic Sanction, which rival rulers soon challenged.
options.label: key
options.why: Emperor Charles VI died in October 1740; his daughter Maria Theresa claimed the Habsburg lands under the Pragmatic Sanction, and Prussia, Bavaria, and France challenged her in the War of the Austrian Succession.

options.text: The death of the childless Charles II of Spain led France and Austria to contest the inheritance of the Spanish crown and empire.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This was the War of the Spanish Succession, which began in 1701, not the dispute of 1740.

options.text: Rival candidates backed by France and by Russia and Austria fought over the elective throne of Poland after Augustus II died.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The War of the Polish Succession (1733 to 1735) was over before 1740 and did not concern the Habsburg inheritance.

options.text: The exclusion of the Catholic Stuarts from the British throne left a Jacobite claim to the crown that France was willing to support.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Jacobite claim was real but concerned Britain, not the Habsburg succession that gave Frederick his opening in Silesia.

facts: Emperor Charles VI died in 1740, and his daughter Maria Theresa succeeded to the Habsburg lands under the Pragmatic Sanction.
The War of the Austrian Succession lasted from 1740 to 1748.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton links Frederick's move to an expected disputed succession and a 'scramble' in 1740, which refers to the Habsburg inheritance.
design.evidence_quote: The succession was about to be disputed, and a scramble might be expected.

items.stem: Frederick's seizure of Silesia, as described in the excerpt, most closely resembles which later eighteenth-century development?

options.text: Prussia, Russia, and Austria annexing territory from a weakened Poland in 1772
options.label: key
options.why: The First Partition of Poland was another case of strong monarchies taking land from a weaker state for reasons of state power, as Acton describes in 1740.

options.text: The French National Assembly's 1790 declaration that France renounced all wars waged for the purpose of conquest
options.label: reversal
options.why: The renunciation of conquest rejected the very practice of unprovoked territorial seizure that the excerpt describes.

options.text: Catherine the Great's 1785 Charter of the Nobility confirming noble privileges and exemptions from state taxation
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The charter was a domestic grant of privilege to nobles, not a seizure of territory from another state.

options.text: Joseph II's 1781 Edict of Toleration granting Protestant and Orthodox subjects in Habsburg lands the right to worship
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The edict was a religious reform within the Habsburg lands, not an act of territorial conquest.

facts: In the First Partition of Poland in 1772, Prussia, Russia, and Austria annexed Polish territory.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton presents the seizure as conquest by a strong state that faced no law above it, a pattern repeated in the partition of Poland.
design.evidence_quote: Frederic was ambitious, and he was strong enough to gratify his ambition.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following was a later consequence of the seizure of Silesia described in the excerpt?

options.text: Austria's aim of regaining Silesia helped bring it into alliance with France before the Seven Years' War.
options.label: key
options.why: Maria Theresa's wish to recover Silesia led Austria to ally with its old rival France in the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756, and the Seven Years' War followed.

options.text: Austria joined Britain in the 1750s to guarantee Prussian control of Silesia against threats from France and from Russia.
options.label: reversal
options.why: In 1756 Britain allied with Prussia, while Austria joined France and Russia to try to take Silesia back.

options.text: Prussia's defeat at Jena in 1806 led to reforms of its army and the abolition of serfdom under Stein and Hardenberg.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Prussian reforms came from the Napoleonic defeat, not from the conquest of Silesia decades earlier.

options.text: Frederick's victory persuaded Maria Theresa to abandon centralizing reforms and restore the privileges of the Bohemian estates.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Losing Silesia pushed Maria Theresa toward stronger centralization of taxes and administration, not away from it.

facts: In the Diplomatic Revolution of 1756, Austria allied with France and Britain allied with Prussia.
The Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763) ended with the Peace of Hubertusburg, under which Prussia kept Silesia.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes Frederick taking Silesia from Austria in 1740, which led Austria to seek its recovery in later wars.
design.evidence_quote: Frederic at once made himself master of Silesia.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most limits the excerpt's usefulness as evidence of how Europeans in 1740 judged Frederick's seizure of Silesia?

options.text: Acton wrote about 160 years later and does not quote any participant from 1740.
options.label: key
options.why: The context line dates the lecture to about 1899. Acton gives his own summary of opinion in 1740 instead of quoting contemporaries, so he is reconstructing their views rather than recording them.

options.text: Acton was British, and Britain fought against Prussia as an ally of Austria throughout the Seven Years' War.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Britain was Prussia's ally in the Seven Years' War, so this claimed source of bias is false.

options.text: Acton lectured at Cambridge, so the excerpt was meant mainly to persuade Parliament to adopt a pro-German foreign policy.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the credit line or context line identifies Parliament as the audience or a policy goal as the purpose.

options.text: Acton relied only on Frederick's own memoirs, so the excerpt simply repeats the official Prussian justification for the war.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt and credit line do not identify Acton's sources, and his ironic tone does not simply repeat a Prussian defense.

facts: Frederick II invaded Silesia in 1740.
Britain was allied with Prussia during the Seven Years' War (1756 to 1763).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says Acton gave the lecture around 1899 about events of 1740, and the excerpt contains no quotations from 1740.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Acton's main claim about the absolutism that arose in Northern Europe around the time of England's revolution settlement?

options.text: A new absolutism arose in which the state ruled for its own sake rather than alongside the church.
options.label: key
options.why: Acton says theological monarchy had done its time and that henceforth the state oppressed for its own sake, a new type of military monarchy.

options.text: The absolutism of Russia and Prussia continued the religious kingship practiced by Philip II and Louis XIV in earlier decades.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton says the new type is not to be confounded with that of Henry VIII, Philip II, or Lewis XIV.

options.text: Military monarchs in northern Europe governed through noble assemblies that limited the ruler's control over taxation and armies.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Acton describes government as undivided and uncontrolled, not limited by assemblies.

options.text: Peter the Great's reforms faced resistance from Orthodox clergy and from Old Believers who rejected Western customs.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Opposition to Peter existed, but the excerpt does not make this claim; it describes a new form of state power.

facts: Peter the Great ruled Russia from 1682 (sole rule from 1696) to 1725.
Frederick William I ruled Prussia from 1713 to 1740.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton contrasts the old theological monarchy with a new military monarchy in which the state rules for its own sake.
design.evidence_quote: Church and State had oppressed mankind together; henceforth the State oppressed for its own sake.

items.stem: The rise of the military monarchy at Petersburg and Berlin that Acton describes is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Rivalry among European states in which standing armies were needed to win territory, as in wars against Sweden
options.label: key
options.why: Russia built its army and navy during the Great Northern War against Sweden, and Prussia's expanded army let it seize Silesia; state competition drove military state-building.

options.text: The spread of constitutional limits on royal power after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 established Parliament's supremacy in England
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton presents the English settlement as the opposite of military monarchy, so it is a contrast, not the context for it.

options.text: The revolutions of 1848, which led Prussian and Russian monarchs to rely on troops to crush liberal and national uprisings
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The revolutions of 1848 came more than a century after the reigns of Peter the Great and Frederick William I.

options.text: The growth of Atlantic commerce that made Amsterdam and London the leading centers of banking and overseas trade in Europe
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Dutch and English commercial growth was real, but it does not explain the military absolutism of Russia and Prussia.

facts: The Great Northern War (1700-1721) ended with the Treaty of Nystad, which gave Russia Baltic territories taken from Sweden.
Prussia under Frederick II seized Silesia from Austria beginning in 1740.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton links the new state's power to millions of bayonets at Petersburg and Berlin, pointing to military competition among states.
design.evidence_quote: That is the tremendous power, supported by millions of bayonets, which grew up in the days of which I have been speaking at Petersburg

items.stem: Acton's contrast between Northern European military monarchy and England's revolution settlement reflects which difference between Prussia and England in the late 1600s and 1700s?

options.text: Prussian rulers raised armies and taxes without estates' consent, while English kings needed Parliament's approval
options.label: key
options.why: Hohenzollern rulers reduced the power of the estates and taxed to fund a standing army, while the English Bill of Rights of 1689 required Parliament's consent for taxes and a peacetime army.

options.text: England maintained a far larger peacetime standing army than Prussia, which relied chiefly on part-time local militias for defense
options.label: reversal
options.why: Prussia was known for an unusually large standing army relative to its population; England distrusted standing armies.

options.text: Prussian nobles were barred from the officer corps, while English gentry families monopolized command of the royal army and navy
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Prussian Junker nobility dominated the officer corps, serving the crown in exchange for privileges over their peasants.

options.text: Prussia enforced strict Lutheran uniformity and expelled dissenters, while England granted full civil rights to Catholics after 1689
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Prussia welcomed Huguenot refugees in 1685, and England's Toleration Act of 1689 excluded Catholics.

facts: The English Bill of Rights (1689) required parliamentary consent for taxation and for a standing army in peacetime.
Prussian Junkers dominated the officer corps of the Prussian army in the 1700s.
The Edict of Potsdam (1685) invited Huguenot refugees to Brandenburg-Prussia.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton places the rise of undivided, uncontrolled military monarchy alongside 'our revolution settlement,' inviting a comparison of Prussian absolutism with English constitutionalism.
design.evidence_quote: the original theory, that government must be undivided and uncontrolled, began to prevail

items.stem: Which of the following most limits the usefulness of Acton's lecture as evidence about Prussian and Russian government in the early 1700s?

options.text: Worry about the German Empire's power in his own day may have shaped how he judged Prussia's earlier rulers
options.label: key
options.why: Speaking around 1899, after German unification and amid rising Anglo-German rivalry, Acton calls Berlin's power the greatest danger to his own people, which may color his reading of the earlier period.

options.text: As a contemporary witness to Peter the Great's reign, he relied on personal memories that were colored by court rivalries
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Acton lectured about 1899, nearly two centuries after Peter's reign, so he was not a witness.

options.text: As a paid adviser to the Russian tsars, he aimed to portray Petersburg as more advanced than its Prussian rival in Berlin
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context identifies him as a Cambridge historian, and he says Berlin's minds were abler than Petersburg's.

options.text: Because he admired military monarchy, he exaggerated its successes in order to urge Britain to adopt a similar system
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton calls this power the greatest danger to be encountered, which is a warning, not admiration.

facts: The German Empire was proclaimed in 1871 under Prussian leadership.
Germany passed a naval law in 1898 that began a large fleet expansion, adding to Anglo-German rivalry.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context dates the lecture to about 1899, and Acton ends by calling Berlin's power a present danger, showing his concerns at the time he was writing.
design.evidence_quote: it is the greatest danger that remains to be encountered by the Anglo-Saxon race

items.stem: Which of the following policies of Peter the Great best illustrates Acton's description of the new government as "the teacher of knowledge"?

options.text: Peter founded schools of mathematics and navigation to train men for state and military service
options.label: key
options.why: Peter set up the Moscow School of Mathematics and Navigation in 1701 and later an Academy of Sciences, using state-directed education to serve military and administrative needs.

options.text: Peter restored the independent authority of the Orthodox patriarch so the church could direct education across Russia
options.label: reversal
options.why: Peter abolished the patriarchate and placed the church under the state-controlled Holy Synod in 1721.

options.text: Peter emancipated the serfs so that peasants could attend new village schools and enter the growing urban workforce
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Serfdom grew stronger under Peter; Alexander II emancipated the serfs in 1861.

options.text: Peter allowed private merchants to establish universities free from state oversight on the model of Dutch cities
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Petrine education was directed by the state, matching Acton's point that the state alone governs.

facts: Peter the Great founded the School of Mathematics and Navigation in Moscow in 1701.
Peter replaced the patriarchate with the Holy Synod in 1721.
Alexander II emancipated the Russian serfs in 1861.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton lists the state's roles as guide, promoter of wealth and teacher of knowledge, which matches Peter's state-run technical schools.
design.evidence_quote: the intellectual guide of the nation, the promoter of wealth, the teacher of knowledge, the guardian of morality

items.stem: The excerpt says the Great Depression hit Germany hard because the economy depended on short-term loans from the United States. Which of the following best explains that dependence?

options.text: American loans under the Dawes Plan of 1924 had financed both German recovery and reparations payments.
options.label: key
options.why: After the 1923 crisis, the Dawes Plan restructured reparations and brought in American loans that funded German recovery. When the loans were recalled after 1929, the collapse the excerpt describes followed.

options.text: Germany's industries had come to rely on trade with the Soviet Union after the two states signed the Treaty of Rapallo in 1922.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Rapallo did reopen German-Soviet relations, but it has nothing to do with American short-term loans, which is the dependence the excerpt names.

options.text: German factories depended on raw materials shipped from African colonies that Germany still governed as League of Nations mandates.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Treaty of Versailles took away Germany's colonies, and the mandates went to other powers. Germany governed none of them.

options.text: Weimar governments had nationalized most heavy industry, so a fall in state revenue immediately shut down the country's factories.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Weimar Germany kept a private industrial economy, and the excerpt blames recalled foreign loans, not state ownership.

facts: The Dawes Plan of 1924 rescheduled German reparations and brought large American loans into Germany.
After the Wall Street crash of October 1929, American lenders recalled short-term loans to Germany.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt ties Germany's suffering to its dependence on short-term American loans that were later recalled.
design.evidence_quote: the German economy's well-being depended on short-term loans from the United States

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would most directly support the excerpt's claim that the economic collapse made Hitler's rise to power possible?

options.text: The Nazi share of the Reichstag vote rose from under 3 percent in 1928 to about 37 percent in July 1932.
options.label: key
options.why: The Nazi vote jumped as unemployment climbed after 1929. That timing fits the excerpt's claim that desperate voters turned to the NSDAP.

options.text: Hitler's failed Beer Hall Putsch in Munich in 1923 showed that the Nazis could not seize power by armed force alone.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is true, but the putsch came before the Depression. It does not link economic collapse to Nazi success.

options.text: The Nazi vote fell in the November 1932 election, and the party had to rely on conservative elites to gain office in 1933.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Even though the Depression was still going on, this evidence points to political deals rather than economic desperation alone. It would qualify the excerpt's argument, not support it.

options.text: Hitler set out his racial and expansionist goals in Mein Kampf, which he wrote while imprisoned at Landsberg in 1924.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This describes Nazi ideology. It is not evidence that the economic crisis gave the party its mass support.

facts: The NSDAP won about 2.6 percent of the vote in 1928, about 18 percent in September 1930, and about 37 percent in July 1932.
German unemployment peaked in 1932 during the Great Depression.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt argues that the Depression made Hitler's rise possible and that desperate voters chose extreme solutions, a claim that election results from 1928 to 1932 would back up.
design.evidence_quote: Had it not been for the economic collapse that began with the Wall Street stock market crash of October 1929, Hitler probably would not have come to power.

items.stem: The unemployment crisis described in the excerpt most directly shaped which of the following policies of the Nazi regime in Germany after 1933?

options.text: Rearmament and public works programs lowered unemployment while preparing Germany for war.
options.label: key
options.why: The Nazi regime cut the unemployment of the early 1930s through state spending on road building, such as the autobahns, and on rearmament, which was also part of its preparation for expansion.

options.text: Germany joined the European Coal and Steel Community to rebuild its heavy industry through joint markets.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: West Germany joined the ECSC in the early 1950s, after the Second World War.

options.text: Independent trade unions gained new bargaining rights as the government expanded collective wage agreements.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The Nazis abolished independent trade unions in May 1933 and put workers under the German Labor Front.

options.text: Germany ended its reparations by signing the Locarno treaties, which guaranteed its western borders with France and Belgium.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Locarno treaties of 1925 dealt with borders, not reparations. Reparations were effectively ended at Lausanne in 1932, before Hitler took office.

facts: The Nazi regime abolished independent trade unions in May 1933.
Nazi Germany reduced unemployment in the 1930s through public works such as the autobahns and through rearmament.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt's unemployment figures, which peaked at 29.9 percent in 1932, show the crisis that the Nazi economic programs after 1933 set out to address.
design.evidence_quote: and, at its peak, to 29.9 percent in 1932

items.stem: The excerpt's reference to middle-class Germans who had lost status since the end of World War I is best understood in the context of which development?

options.text: Hyperinflation in 1923 had destroyed the value of many middle-class savings and pensions.
options.label: key
options.why: The hyperinflation of 1923 wiped out the savings and fixed incomes of many middle-class Germans. This left many of them bitter toward the Weimar Republic and open to Nazi appeals.

options.text: Bismarck's social insurance laws of the 1880s had shifted the cost of workers' pensions onto middle-class taxpayers.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Bismarck's laws came decades before World War I, so they cannot explain a loss of status that began after 1918.

options.text: The Kulturkampf of the 1870s had stripped Catholic professionals of positions in the Prussian civil service.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Kulturkampf was a conflict between Bismarck and the Catholic Church in the 1870s, long before the postwar period the excerpt describes.

options.text: The Congress of Vienna had restored aristocratic privileges that excluded middle-class Germans from political office.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Congress of Vienna met in 1814 and 1815. It has no connection to status lost after World War I.

facts: German hyperinflation peaked in 1923, when the mark became nearly worthless.
The hyperinflation wiped out savings and fixed incomes held by many middle-class Germans.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt names middle-class Germans who had lost status since World War I, which points to the postwar economic shocks of the Weimar period.
design.evidence_quote: members of the middle class who had been hurt by the Depression or had lost status since the end of World War I

items.stem: Which of the following is a possible limitation of using this excerpt, written in the mid-1990s, to explain how Hitler came to power?

options.text: It may understate how conservative elites around Hindenburg helped make Hitler chancellor.
options.label: key
options.why: The excerpt puts its weight on economic collapse and voter desperation. Hitler became chancellor in January 1933 because President Hindenburg appointed him on the advice of conservative politicians, a factor the passage does not discuss.

options.text: As an account written during the 1930s, it reflects the wartime propaganda that the United States directed at Nazi Germany.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The credit line dates the work to 1996, with research completed in 1995, so it is not a contemporary account from the 1930s.

options.text: Because it is a U.S. government work, it is required by law to defend American banks from blame for the German collapse.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the source supports such a requirement, and the excerpt actually blames the recall of American loans for Germany's collapse.

options.text: It relies only on Goebbels's own propaganda claims, so its unemployment figures cannot be checked against other evidence.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt mentions Goebbels's campaign, but it does not say its statistics come from him. German unemployment figures can be checked against other evidence.

facts: President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Hitler chancellor on January 30, 1933.
Conservative politicians, including Franz von Papen, urged Hindenburg to appoint Hitler.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line and credit line show a 1990s reference work, and the passage it gives explains Hitler's rise mainly through economic collapse and voter appeal.
design.evidence_quote: In times of desperation, voters are ready for extreme solutions, and the NSDAP exploited the situation.

items.stem: Keynes's point of view in the excerpt was most likely shaped by which of the following?

options.text: His experience as a Treasury adviser at the peace conference, focused on Europe's finances
options.label: key
options.why: The context line says Keynes was a British economist working for the Treasury at the 1919 conference. That role explains why he sees the main dangers as financial and economic, in food, coal and transport.

options.text: His duty as a British official to publicly defend the peace terms that Lloyd George had negotiated in Paris
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt attacks the reparations campaign as serious political unwisdom by the statesmen, Lloyd George among them. It does not defend the terms.

options.text: His socialist belief that capitalism itself, not the peace terms, caused Europe's postwar poverty
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Keynes was a liberal economist, not a socialist. The excerpt blames the peacemakers' choices, not capitalism.

options.text: His support for Wilson's principle of national self-determination as the basis for new borders
options.label: reversal
options.why: Keynes says the perils lay not in frontiers or sovereignties. Borders built on self-determination are exactly what he treats as less important.

facts: Keynes represented the British Treasury at the Paris Peace Conference in 1919.
Keynes resigned from the British delegation in June 1919 in protest over the peace terms.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line names his Treasury role at the conference, and the text puts economic problems ahead of political ones.
design.evidence_quote: were not political or territorial but financial and economic

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Keynes's main claim in the excerpt?

options.text: The peacemakers stressed borders over the economic problems that most threatened Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Keynes argues that Lloyd George and Wilson did not see that Europe's worst problems were financial and economic rather than territorial.

options.text: Germany should pay the full costs of the war so that Britain and France could rebuild their economies
options.label: reversal
options.why: Keynes calls the campaign to make Germany pay the general costs of the war one of the most serious acts of political unwisdom.

options.text: Disputes over frontiers and the sovereignty of new states posed the greatest danger to Europe's future
options.label: reversal
options.why: Keynes says the perils lay not in frontiers or sovereignties but in food, coal and transport.

options.text: Lloyd George and Wilson deliberately sought to wreck the German economy to keep Germany from rearming
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Keynes blames the leaders for failing to understand the problem. He never accuses them of a deliberate plan to ruin Germany or connects reparations to rearmament.

facts: David Lloyd George was British prime minister and Woodrow Wilson was United States president at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt contrasts the political and territorial matters the leaders focused on with the economic dangers Keynes saw.
design.evidence_quote: the perils of the future lay not in frontiers or sovereignties but in food, coal, and transport

items.stem: The campaign that Keynes criticizes in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Allied publics and governments sought compensation for the huge losses of the war
options.label: key
options.why: The Allies had suffered enormous losses and run up large war debts, and there was strong public pressure in Britain and France to make Germany pay. Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles provided the legal basis for reparations.

options.text: The collapse of world trade and mass unemployment that followed the American stock market crash of 1929
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Keynes published in 1919, a decade before the crash and the Great Depression.

options.text: Soviet Russia's demand at the Paris conference that Germany repay Russia's losses on the Eastern Front
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Soviet Russia had left the war through the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in 1918 and was not represented at the Paris Peace Conference.

options.text: The League of Nations' creation of mandates to govern former Ottoman and German territories
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The mandate system did come out of the peace settlement, but it was a territorial arrangement. It does not explain the campaign to recover war costs from Germany.

facts: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles (1919) held Germany and its allies responsible for the loss and damage caused by the war.
The Treaty of Versailles was signed on June 28, 1919.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Keynes refers to a campaign to secure the general costs of the war from Germany, which reflected Allied demands for compensation.
design.evidence_quote: the campaign for securing out of Germany the general costs of the war

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following developments in the 1920s most directly reflected the concerns Keynes expressed in the excerpt?

options.text: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in 1923 after Germany fell behind on payments
options.label: key
options.why: The Ruhr occupation came out of the reparations dispute, centered on Germany's coal-rich industrial region, and helped bring on the hyperinflation of 1923. It reflects the financial dangers and the stakes in coal that Keynes stressed.

options.text: Germany accepted its western borders with France and Belgium in the Locarno treaties of 1925
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Locarno settled frontiers, the kind of issue Keynes considered less dangerous. It was not an economic crisis caused by reparations.

options.text: Mussolini's Fascists took power in Italy after the March on Rome, citing a mutilated victory
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Italian Fascism drew on territorial grievances and domestic unrest, not on German reparations.

options.text: The Soviet Union launched its first Five-Year Plan in 1928 to industrialize through central planning
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Five-Year Plan was an internal Soviet economic policy and had nothing to do with reparations from Germany.

facts: France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in 1923 after Germany defaulted on reparations deliveries.
German hyperinflation peaked in 1923.
The Locarno treaties were signed in 1925.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Keynes warns that reparations and economic matters such as coal were the real dangers, and the Ruhr crisis bore that out.
design.evidence_quote: the perils of the future lay not in frontiers or sovereignties but in food, coal, and transport

items.stem: EXTRA: Which of the following is a limitation of the excerpt as evidence of how reparations actually affected the German economy?

options.text: Keynes wrote before the final reparations total was set and payments began
options.label: key
options.why: The book appeared in December 1919. The Reparation Commission did not fix the total until 1921, so Keynes was predicting effects, not reporting them.

options.text: Keynes had no direct knowledge of the negotiations because he did not attend the Paris conference
options.label: reversal
options.why: The context line states that Keynes worked for the British Treasury at the 1919 Paris Peace Conference.

options.text: Keynes wrote after the Great Depression, so he blamed reparations for problems caused by the crash
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The book was published in 1919, a decade before the Great Depression began.

options.text: Keynes was a German economist who wanted to win sympathy for his own country's position
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The context line identifies Keynes as a British economist who worked for the British Treasury.

facts: The total reparations bill of 132 billion gold marks was set in 1921 (London Schedule of Payments).
The Economic Consequences of the Peace was published in December 1919.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line dates publication to December 1919, before reparations were fixed and paid.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes Motley's main claim about the image-breaking in the Netherlands in 1566?

options.text: It was destructive but understandable, since the images had become symbols of persecution.
options.label: key
options.why: Motley regrets the loss to art but says it is impossible to censure the deed very severely because the statues were associated with remorseless persecution.

options.text: It was mainly a campaign of looting in which crowds stripped churches of valuables to enrich themselves and their towns.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Motley says directly that the churches were rifled not for the purpose of plunder but of destruction.

options.text: It was a wholly admirable act of reform that caused no real loss, because the statues had no artistic or cultural value.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Motley calls the deed brutal and says Art must forever weep over the loss, so he does not call it wholly admirable.

options.text: It was a carefully planned operation directed by noble leaders who wanted to force Philip II to abandon royal authority.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt presents a sudden storm in which the people arose; it says nothing of noble planning or a goal of ending royal authority.

facts: A wave of iconoclasm (the Beeldenstorm) swept churches in the Habsburg Netherlands in August 1566.
The Netherlands were ruled by Philip II of Spain at the time, with Margaret of Parma as regent.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Motley balances regret for the destruction against his statement that the deed cannot be censured very severely because of its link to persecution.
design.evidence_quote: it is impossible to censure very severely the spirit which prompted the brutal, but not ferocious deed

items.stem: Which of the following pieces of evidence would best support Motley's claim that church images had become associated with persecution in the Netherlands before 1566?

options.text: Habsburg edicts against heresy in the Netherlands had sent many Protestants to execution.
options.label: key
options.why: Charles V and Philip II enforced harsh anti-heresy placards in the Low Countries, under which many Protestants were executed; this backs Motley's reference to long persecution.

options.text: Spanish troops sacked Antwerp in 1576, killing thousands of residents and destroying much of the city's property.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Spanish Fury of 1576 came ten years after the image-breaking and cannot explain feelings that existed before 1566.

options.text: Zwinglian authorities in Zurich removed images from churches in the 1520s through orderly town council decisions.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Zurich did remove images in the 1520s, but this says nothing about persecution in the Netherlands or why people there linked statues to it.

options.text: Wealthy Netherlandish merchants had funded many altarpieces and chapels in parish churches over several generations.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This would support Motley's point about richly adorned churches, not his claim that the images were tied to persecution.

facts: Charles V issued harsh placards against heresy in the Netherlands, including the edict of 1550, under which Protestants could be executed.
The first Protestant martyrs of the Reformation were burned in Brussels in 1523.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Motley says the statues were associated with the remorseless persecution that had desolated the provinces, so evidence of executions for heresy supports him.
design.evidence_quote: associated as they were with the remorseless persecution which had so long desolated the provinces

items.stem: Which of the following was a direct consequence of the image-breaking described in the excerpt?

options.text: Philip II sent the Duke of Alba with an army to restore order and punish heresy.
options.label: key
options.why: In response to the 1566 unrest, Philip II sent Alba in 1567; Alba set up the Council of Troubles, and his harsh rule helped turn unrest into the Dutch Revolt.

options.text: Philip II granted Calvinists in the Netherlands legal freedom of worship in order to end the unrest quickly.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Philip II answered with military repression, not toleration; he refused to allow Protestant worship.

options.text: The Peace of Augsburg allowed princes in the Netherlands to choose between Lutheranism and Catholicism for their lands.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Peace of Augsburg dates from 1555, before the image-breaking, and it concerned princes in the Holy Roman Empire choosing Lutheranism or Catholicism.

options.text: Henry IV issued the Edict of Nantes, granting the Netherlands' Calvinists the right to hold fortified towns.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Edict of Nantes (1598) gave rights to French Huguenots, not to Dutch Calvinists, and it was not a response to 1566.

facts: The Duke of Alba arrived in the Netherlands with Spanish troops in 1567 and set up the Council of Troubles.
The Edict of Nantes was issued by Henry IV of France in 1598.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes the destruction of churches in nearly every province, which led Philip II to respond with military repression.
design.evidence_quote: Hardly a province or a town escaped.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following developments of the 1550s and 1560s most directly provided the context for the events described in the excerpt?

options.text: The rapid spread of Calvinism in the Low Countries, including open-air hedge preaching
options.label: key
options.why: Calvinism, which rejected religious images, spread quickly in the Netherlands, and crowded open-air sermons in the summer of 1566 came just before the attacks on church statues.

options.text: The rise of the Anabaptist kingdom at Münster, where radicals seized the city and imposed communal ownership
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Münster rebellion took place in 1534 and 1535, decades before the period named in the stem.

options.text: The outbreak of the Thirty Years' War after Protestant nobles in Bohemia threw imperial officials from a window
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Defenestration of Prague and the start of the Thirty Years' War came in 1618, after 1566.

options.text: The English Parliament's Act of Supremacy making the monarch head of a national church independent of Rome
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The English church settlements concerned England's church and do not explain popular attacks on images in the Habsburg Netherlands.

facts: Calvinist open-air hedge preaching drew large crowds in the Netherlands in the summer of 1566.
Calvinist theology condemned religious images as idolatry.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt describes a reforming attack on statues and chapels, which reflects the Calvinist rejection of images then spreading in the provinces.
design.evidence_quote: Humanity must regret that the reforming is thus always ready to degenerate into the destructive principle

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following most likely limits the usefulness of Motley's account as evidence about the motives of the 1566 image-breakers?

options.text: His sympathy for the Dutch rebels leads him to excuse the destruction as a reaction to persecution.
options.label: key
options.why: Motley, writing almost three centuries later, refuses to censure the deed severely and ties it to persecution; this sympathetic view may play down other motives, such as Calvinist teaching against idolatry.

options.text: He witnessed the attacks as a young man and so recorded only what happened in the single town where he lived.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context line says Motley published in 1856 as an American historian, so he could not have been an eyewitness in 1566.

options.text: He wrote as a defender of the Catholic Church and so blamed the destruction entirely on foreign Spanish agitators.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Motley criticizes wealthy penitence buying absolution and excuses the image-breakers; he does not defend the Church or blame Spanish agitators.

options.text: He relied only on official Spanish government reports, which recorded the losses but not the crowds' intentions.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the excerpt or the context line shows what sources Motley used.

facts: Motley published The Rise of the Dutch Republic in 1856, about 290 years after the 1566 iconoclasm.
The Dutch Revolt against Philip II's rule grew out of the unrest of the 1560s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Motley's refusal to condemn the deed and his comment that the statues had grown human and hateful show a sympathetic view that shapes how he explains motives.
design.evidence_quote: They had grown human and hateful, so that the people arose and devoted them to indiscriminate massacre.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the author's main argument about Catholic reform in the early decades of the Reformation?

options.text: Reform stalled before Trent largely because the papal court depended on revenues that reform would cut off.
options.label: key
options.why: Acton says reformers faced officials 'for whom reform was ruin' and that Rome lived on money from indulgences, dispensations, and patronage that reform would damage.

options.text: Catholic leaders mounted a swift, coordinated counteroffensive against Luther that halted the spread of Protestant ideas in Germany.
options.label: reversal
options.why: Acton says the Reformation spread 'without arousing any strong reaction among Catholics, or inspiring them with a policy.'

options.text: Cardinals of the period were indifferent to abuses in the Church and saw no reason to change the practices of the papal court.
options.label: overstated
options.why: Acton says religious cardinals 'knew, and acknowledged, and deplored' the Church's defects and swore oaths at conclaves to check abuses.

options.text: The Fifth Lateran Council succeeded in abolishing indulgences, but its reforms were later undone by the Protestant break with Rome.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Acton says that at the Lateran Council the same men allowed indulgences to be renewed, so the council did not abolish them.

facts: The Fifth Lateran Council met from 1512 to 1517 under Julius II and Leo X and did not carry out major reform.
The Council of Trent met from 1545 to 1563.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton contrasts sincere reformers with Curia officials whose income depended on the abuses, and ties this to Rome's revenues.
design.evidence_quote: those who held the language of Erasmus were confronted by a resisting body of officials for whom reform was ruin

items.stem: Which of the following would best support the author's claim that "Rome flourished on money obtained from the nations"?

options.text: Leo X sponsored an indulgence campaign in the German lands to help pay for rebuilding St. Peter's Basilica in Rome.
options.label: key
options.why: The indulgence campaign preached in Germany, which Luther attacked in 1517, moved money from German believers to Rome. That is exactly what Acton describes.

options.text: Ignatius of Loyola founded the Society of Jesus, which built schools and sent missionaries to Asia and the Americas.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: This is real Catholic Reformation history, but Jesuit schools and missions say nothing about Rome drawing revenue from other countries.

options.text: The Council of Trent reaffirmed the seven sacraments and declared that the Latin Vulgate was the authoritative text of scripture.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These are doctrinal decrees of Trent. They do not show Rome profiting from fees and indulgences.

options.text: Imperial troops of Charles V sacked Rome in 1527, looting churches and briefly holding Pope Clement VII as a prisoner.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The Sack of Rome shows wealth being taken from Rome, not Rome collecting money from the nations.

facts: Leo X proclaimed an indulgence to fund the rebuilding of St. Peter's Basilica, preached in Germany by Johann Tetzel.
Luther's Ninety-Five Theses of 1517 attacked this indulgence preaching.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton names indulgences among the sources of the money Rome drew from the nations. The St. Peter's indulgence in Germany is a concrete example.
design.evidence_quote: Rome flourished on money obtained from the nations in return for ecclesiastical treasures, for promotion and patronage, for indulgences and dispensations

items.stem: The author's description of a Church weakened by "secular interests, profane literature and art" is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Renaissance popes acted as Italian territorial rulers and lavish patrons of humanist art and learning.
options.label: key
options.why: Popes such as Julius II and Leo X fought Italian wars and spent heavily on art and humanist culture. This is the worldliness Acton blames for spiritual slackness.

options.text: Rival popes in Avignon and Rome were still competing for the loyalty of Europe's monarchs and their clergy.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Great Schism ended in 1417, about a century before the events in the excerpt.

options.text: Baroque artists, encouraged by the Council of Trent, were filling Roman churches with dramatic and emotional religious images.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Baroque religious art came after Trent and served Catholic renewal. It was not part of the earlier worldliness Acton describes.

options.text: Enlightenment philosophes were spreading deist ideas that questioned revealed religion among educated Europeans.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Deism and the Enlightenment belong to the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, not the early sixteenth century.

facts: Leo X (pope 1513-1521) was a Medici and a major patron of Renaissance art and humanist learning.
Julius II (pope 1503-1513) led papal armies in the Italian Wars and began the rebuilding of St. Peter's in 1506.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton links the slackness of the early-sixteenth-century Church to secular interests and to profane literature and art, which points to the Renaissance papacy.
design.evidence_quote: Under the influence of secular interests, profane literature and art, it was a time of slackness in spiritual life.

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following later sixteenth-century developments most directly addressed the problems of church government that the author describes?

options.text: The Council of Trent ordered bishops to reside in their dioceses and to found seminaries for training priests.
options.label: key
options.why: Trent's disciplinary decrees targeted the abuses of an 'ill-governed Church' that Acton says earlier reformers deplored but could not fix.

options.text: The Peace of Augsburg allowed each German prince to choose whether Catholicism or Lutheranism would be the religion of his lands.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 1555 settlement dealt with religious division in the Empire, not with the internal government of the Catholic Church.

options.text: The papacy issued an Index of Prohibited Books to keep Protestant and other heretical writings out of the hands of Catholic readers.
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Index was aimed at heresy, not at the financial and administrative abuses of the papal court.

options.text: Henry VIII's Act of Supremacy made the English monarch head of the church in England and ended payments to Rome.
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The 1534 act was a break with Rome, not a reform of the Catholic Church from within.

facts: The Council of Trent (1545-1563) required bishops to live in their dioceses and ordered seminaries founded to train clergy.
The Peace of Augsburg (1555) let German princes choose between Catholicism and Lutheranism.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton describes an ill-governed Church whose defects reformers deplored but failed to correct. Trent's disciplinary decrees later took up those defects.
design.evidence_quote: deplored, as sincerely as Adrian VI, the growing defects of the ill-governed Church

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following best explains why the "loss of Germany" mentioned in the excerpt reduced the revenues available to Rome?

options.text: Lutheran princes ended payments to Rome and took over church lands in their own territories.
options.label: key
options.why: German princes who adopted Lutheranism stopped money flowing to Rome and took over church property. This cut off the revenues Acton describes.

options.text: Charles V seized papal estates throughout the Holy Roman Empire to punish Rome after the Diet of Worms in 1521.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Charles V stayed Catholic and condemned Luther in the Edict of Worms. The loss of revenue came from Protestant princes, not the emperor.

options.text: The Thirty Years' War destroyed the German towns that had once supplied the papacy with most of its income from indulgences.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Thirty Years' War began in 1618, long after the loss of Germany that Acton describes.

options.text: The German Peasants' War of 1525 abolished the tithe across the empire and permanently ended church taxation of rural villages.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Peasants' War was crushed in 1525 and did not abolish church dues across the Empire.

facts: The Edict of Worms (1521) issued under Charles V declared Luther an outlaw.
Lutheran princes such as those of Saxony and Hesse took over church property in their lands in the 1520s and 1530s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Acton says that once Germany was lost, Rome's remaining revenue sources became more necessary, which implies German money had stopped flowing to Rome.
design.evidence_quote: With the loss of Germany the sources of revenue that remained became more necessary

items.stem: The image and slogan on this September 1914 magazine cover were most likely intended to

options.text: persuade British men to volunteer for service in the army
options.label: key
options.why: The uniformed figure points straight at the viewer beside the words 'Your country needs YOU.' In September 1914 Britain was raising a mass army from volunteers, so the cover is a recruiting appeal.

options.text: build public support for a new law requiring all able-bodied men to serve
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Britain did not pass conscription until the Military Service Act of 1916. In 1914 the appeal was for volunteers, not support for a draft law.

options.text: criticize military leaders for drawing Britain into a war on the continent
options.label: reversal
options.why: The cover presents a military leader as a figure of patriotic authority. It supports the war effort and does not criticize it.

options.text: encourage British women to take jobs in factories producing artillery shells
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Nothing in the image is aimed at women or at factory work. Mass recruitment of women into munitions work also came mainly after the shell shortage of 1915.

facts: Britain declared war on Germany on August 4, 1914.
Lord Kitchener became Secretary of State for War in August 1914 and called for large numbers of volunteers.
Britain introduced conscription with the Military Service Act of 1916.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The pointing finger and the slogan addressing the viewer directly, together with the September 1914 date, show the cover was a call for volunteers.
design.evidence_quote: Your country needs YOU

items.stem: Appeals like the one in the image were necessary in Britain in 1914 mainly because Britain, unlike France and Germany,

options.text: had no peacetime conscription and only a small professional army
options.label: key
options.why: France and Germany drafted soldiers in peacetime and had huge trained reserves. Britain relied on a small volunteer professional army, so it had to recruit a mass army by persuasion.

options.text: had lost most of its regular soldiers in the failed Allied landings at Gallipoli
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Gallipoli campaign began in 1915, after this September 1914 cover was printed.

options.text: was bound by the Treaty of Versailles to limit its army to one hundred thousand men
options.label: misattributed
