options.why: The 1919 Treaty of Versailles limited Germany's army, not Britain's, and it was signed after the war.

options.text: had sent nearly all of its trained troops to defend colonies in India and South Africa
options.label: overstated
options.why: Britain did keep garrisons overseas, but it also sent an expeditionary force to France in August 1914. The basic problem was the small size of a volunteer army without conscription.

facts: Before 1914 Britain had no peacetime conscription, unlike France and Germany.
The British Expeditionary Force sent to France in August 1914 was small compared with continental conscript armies.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The cover asks individual viewers to come forward, which reflects Britain's reliance on volunteers rather than a draft in 1914.
design.evidence_quote: Your country needs YOU

items.stem: The magazine cover is best understood as part of which broader development during the First World War?

options.text: Governments' use of propaganda to mobilize entire societies for total war
options.label: key
options.why: All of the warring states used posters, the press and censorship to rally civilians and raise armies. This cover, which became a recruiting poster, is an example of that mass mobilization for total war.

options.text: The scramble for African colonies that European diplomats regulated at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Conference came three decades earlier and dealt with colonial claims, not wartime recruiting at home.

options.text: Rising support for the Second International's call for workers to refuse to fight in a capitalist war
options.label: reversal
options.why: In 1914 most European socialist parties backed their national governments. The cover also calls men to fight, not to refuse.

options.text: The spread of Wilsonian ideals of national self-determination among subject peoples
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Wilson's Fourteen Points date from 1918 and concern the peace settlement, not the call for British volunteers in 1914.

facts: First World War governments used propaganda and state controls to mobilize civilian populations for total war.
Most socialist parties in the Second International supported their national war efforts in 1914.
Wilson issued the Fourteen Points in January 1918.

design.key_evidence_in_source: A popular magazine cover with a patriotic recruiting message, printed weeks after Britain entered the war and later reused as a recruiting poster, shows propaganda aimed at the whole public.
design.evidence_quote: Your country needs YOU

items.stem: Voluntary recruiting of the kind shown in the image was later followed in Britain by which development during the First World War?

options.text: the introduction of military conscription for men in 1916
options.label: key
options.why: Volunteering could not keep up with heavy losses, so Britain passed the Military Service Act in 1916. That law moved Britain from appeals like this one to compulsory service.

options.text: a separate peace with Germany that Britain signed at Brest-Litovsk in 1918
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Bolshevik Russia, not Britain, signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in 1918.

options.text: an end to the fighting by Christmas 1914 after the Allied victory at the Marne
options.label: overstated
options.why: The Battle of the Marne stopped the German advance in September 1914, but it was followed by trench stalemate and years more of war.

options.text: a general strike in 1926 called by British unions to protest wartime army recruiting
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The 1926 General Strike came after the war and supported coal miners in a dispute over wages and hours. It had nothing to do with recruiting.

facts: Britain introduced conscription through the Military Service Act in 1916.
Russia signed the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk with Germany in March 1918.
The British General Strike of 1926 was called in support of coal miners.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1914 cover appeals to individual volunteers, and that voluntary approach was replaced by compulsory service later in the war.
design.evidence_quote: Your country needs YOU

items.stem: The image would be of most limited use to a historian studying which of the following?

options.text: why individual British men actually chose to enlist in 1914
options.label: key
options.why: The cover shows the message presented to the public, not how men received it or why they joined. Their real motives would have to come from sources such as letters, diaries or enlistment records.

options.text: how popular British magazines portrayed military leaders to readers in the first weeks of the war
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: A September 1914 magazine cover showing a uniformed military figure is direct evidence of how the popular press portrayed such leaders.

options.text: visual techniques artists used in 1914 to address viewers directly and personally
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The pointing finger and the word YOU are clear examples of direct address, so the image is very useful for this topic.

options.text: the emphasis on patriotic duty in British appeals for volunteers early in the war
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The slogan's appeal to the country's needs is direct evidence of the patriotic duty theme in early recruiting.

facts: The 'Your Country Needs You' image of Lord Kitchener appeared on London Opinion in September 1914 and was later reused as a recruiting poster.
Britain relied on voluntary enlistment from 1914 until conscription was introduced in 1916.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Because the source is a published appeal by an artist and a magazine, it shows the intended message but not how viewers responded.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the main argument Malthus makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Population tends to grow faster than food production, so scarcity must restrain it
options.label: key
options.why: Malthus says population grows in a geometrical ratio and subsistence only in an arithmetical ratio, so the difficulty of getting food acts as a constant check on population.

options.text: Improvements in farming techniques will let food supplies grow faster than the number of people they feed
options.label: reversal
options.why: This turns the argument around. Malthus calls the power of population far greater than the earth's power to produce food.

options.text: Governments should legally limit marriages and births to keep the population at a fixed size
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt describes a natural check and calls for no law. Malthus did not propose legal limits on marriage.

options.text: Human societies advance steadily toward perfection as reason spreads and removes the causes of want
options.label: misattributed
options.why: This was the optimism of thinkers like Godwin and Condorcet, which Malthus rejected. The excerpt says hardship will be severely felt by a large portion of mankind.

facts: Malthus published An Essay on the Principle of Population anonymously in 1798.
Malthus argued that population grows geometrically while food supply grows arithmetically.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The contrast between geometrical and arithmetical ratios, and the resulting check on population, is the core claim.
design.evidence_quote: Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio. Subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio.

items.stem: Which of the following kinds of evidence would most directly support the argument Malthus makes in the excerpt?

options.text: Records showing rapid population growth followed by soaring grain prices and deaths from famine
options.label: key
options.why: Population growth followed by dearth and higher mortality would show the 'difficulty of subsistence' acting as a check on numbers, just as Malthus predicts.

options.text: Data showing that new crops, crop rotation, and enclosure in Britain raised food output faster than population grew
options.label: reversal
options.why: Food output growing faster than population would undercut Malthus's claim that subsistence cannot keep pace with population.

options.text: Accounts of Enlightenment salons in Paris spreading ideas about natural rights among educated men and women
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Salons were real, but they have nothing to do with the link between population and food supply.

options.text: Evidence that absolutist states such as Prussia expanded standing armies by building more efficient tax systems
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Prussian military and fiscal growth is real history, but it says nothing about population outrunning subsistence.

facts: The eighteenth-century Agricultural Revolution in Britain included new crops such as turnips and clover, crop rotation, and enclosure.
Rising population in early modern Europe often coincided with rising grain prices and subsistence crises.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Malthus claims that the difficulty of getting food constantly checks population, so evidence of dearth following population growth supports him.
design.evidence_quote: This implies a strong and constantly operating check on population from the difficulty of subsistence.

items.stem: Malthus's argument in the excerpt is best understood in the context of which of the following?

options.text: Rapid population growth in eighteenth-century Europe that raised concern about poverty
options.label: key
options.why: Europe's population grew sharply in the 1700s. Falling mortality and better food supplies helped, and the growth raised worries about poverty and poor relief that Malthus addressed in 1798.

options.text: Severe labor shortages after the Black Death that raised wages and weakened serfdom across western Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Black Death and the labor shortages after it came in the fourteenth century, centuries before Malthus wrote.

options.text: Population losses from the Thirty Years' War, which left much of central Europe's farmland deserted and untilled
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Thirty Years' War ended in 1648. Malthus wrote in a time of population growth, not decline.

options.text: Enlightenment optimism about human perfectibility, which the essay embraces as proof that poverty will soon end
options.label: reversal
options.why: Malthus answered Enlightenment optimism by arguing that hardship is permanent. He did not embrace it.

facts: European population grew substantially during the eighteenth century.
The Thirty Years' War ended with the Peace of Westphalia in 1648.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 1798 date and the worry that food shortages will fall on a large portion of mankind place the essay in an era of rapid population growth.
design.evidence_quote: This difficulty must fall somewhere and must necessarily be severely felt by a large portion of mankind.

items.stem: Malthus's idea in the excerpt that limited resources constantly check population growth later most directly influenced which nineteenth-century development?

options.text: Charles Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection
options.label: key
options.why: Darwin said that reading Malthus helped him see how a struggle over scarce resources could drive natural selection. This influence is a standard point in survey courses.

options.text: Karl Marx's theory that class struggle would end in a classless society
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Marx criticized Malthus. He blamed poverty on capitalism, not on a natural law of population.

options.text: Robert Owen's plans for cooperative factory villages such as New Lanark
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Owen's utopian socialism held that better social arrangements could end poverty, which is the opposite of Malthus's pessimism.

options.text: Romantic poets' celebration of untamed nature and emotional experience
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Romanticism was a real nineteenth-century movement, but it did not grow out of Malthus's population theory.

facts: Charles Darwin credited reading Malthus's Essay on population (1838) with helping him form the idea of natural selection, published in On the Origin of Species (1859).
Marx rejected Malthus's population theory.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The 'strong and constantly operating check' from scarce subsistence is the idea Darwin later applied to nature.
design.evidence_quote: a strong and constantly operating check on population from the difficulty of subsistence

items.stem: In the excerpt, Malthus appeals to postulates, mathematical ratios, and a 'law of our nature.' This approach most clearly reflects which Enlightenment tendency?

options.text: Applying the methods of natural science to study human society
options.label: key
options.why: Enlightenment thinkers tried to find natural laws of society the way Newton found laws of physics. Malthus states his postulates and reasons from numbers in the same spirit.

options.text: Relying on scriptural revelation as the final authority on questions of society
options.label: reversal
options.why: Malthus was a clergyman, but the excerpt rests its case on postulates and arithmetic, not on scripture.

options.text: Valuing emotion and intuition over reason as the surest guides to truth
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: This describes Romanticism, which reacted against Enlightenment rationalism. Malthus argues from reasoning and numbers.

options.text: Defending divine-right monarchs' authority to regulate trade and prices
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Divine-right absolutism and royal economic regulation do not appear in the excerpt, which looks for natural laws instead.

facts: Enlightenment thinkers sought to apply scientific reasoning, modeled on Newton's natural laws (Principia, 1687), to society and economics.
Romanticism emerged in the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries partly as a reaction against Enlightenment rationalism.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Malthus's language of postulates, ratios, and a law of nature shows a scientific, law-seeking method applied to society.
design.evidence_quote: A slight acquaintance with numbers will shew the immensity of the first power in comparison of the second.

items.stem: The commitments in Article 5 of the excerpt best reflect which of the following Cold War policies?

options.text: Containment, in which the United States pledged to resist further Soviet expansion in Europe
options.label: key
options.why: By promising to treat an attack on Western European states as an attack on itself, the United States tied itself to defending Western Europe. That is the core of containment, the policy announced in the Truman Doctrine of 1947.

options.text: Détente, in which the superpowers negotiated arms limitations and expanded trade during the 1970s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Détente was a relaxation of tensions in the late 1960s and 1970s. It was not the logic of a 1949 alliance built to deter the Soviet Union.

options.text: Appeasement, in which Western powers accepted territorial demands by an aggressive state to avoid a general war
options.label: reversal
options.why: Appeasement belongs to the 1930s, and the treaty takes the opposite approach: it pledges a joint armed response, not concessions.

options.text: The Brezhnev Doctrine, in which one power claimed a right to intervene to protect socialist rule in allied states
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The Brezhnev Doctrine was the Soviet justification for the 1968 intervention in Czechoslovakia. It does not describe a Western defensive alliance.

facts: The Truman Doctrine of 1947 committed the United States to containing the spread of communism.
The Brezhnev Doctrine was proclaimed in 1968 after the Warsaw Pact invasion of Czechoslovakia.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article 5 says the United States and its partners will regard an armed attack in Europe or North America as an attack on all of them, which puts American power behind Western Europe's defense.
design.evidence_quote: shall be considered an attack against them all

items.stem: Which of the following developments most directly shaped the historical situation in which the treaty was signed in April 1949?

options.text: Soviet pressure in Central Europe, including the blockade of West Berlin and the communist coup in Prague
options.label: key
options.why: The communist takeover in Czechoslovakia in February 1948 and the Soviet blockade of West Berlin, which began in June 1948 and was still in force in April 1949, made Western governments fear Soviet aggression. That fear is why the treaty stresses protecting territorial integrity and political independence.

options.text: The construction of a wall dividing East and West Berlin to halt the flight of East Germans to the West
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961, more than ten years after the treaty was signed.

options.text: The Soviet crushing of the Hungarian uprising, which convinced Western states that Moscow would use force in Europe
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Hungarian uprising happened in 1956, after the alliance already existed.

options.text: The placement of Soviet nuclear missiles in Cuba, which brought the United States and Soviet Union to the brink of war
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Cuban Missile Crisis took place in 1962, so it could not have shaped a treaty signed in 1949.

facts: A communist coup took power in Czechoslovakia in February 1948.
The Soviet blockade of West Berlin lasted from June 1948 to May 1949.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The credit line dates the signing to April 1949, during the Berlin Blockade and soon after the Prague coup, and Article 4 refers to threats to territorial integrity and political independence.
design.evidence_quote: the territorial integrity, political independence or security of any of the Parties is threatened

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a claim made in Article 5 of the excerpt?

options.text: An armed attack on any member in Europe or North America will be treated as an attack on every member
options.label: key
options.why: This restates the opening words of Article 5, which define collective defense.

options.text: Every member is obligated to declare war and send its own troops immediately whenever another member is attacked
options.label: overstated
options.why: Article 5 says each member will take whatever action it deems necessary. Force is included but not required, and the article says nothing about a declaration of war.

options.text: Members may respond to an attack on their own authority without informing the United Nations Security Council
options.label: reversal
options.why: The article requires that attacks and the measures taken in response be reported to the Security Council immediately.

options.text: Members will defend one another against economic and political threats as well as against armed attacks anywhere
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Article 5 covers only armed attacks in Europe or North America. Other threats call for consultation under Article 4, not a defense pledge.

facts: The North Atlantic Treaty was signed in Washington on 4 April 1949 by twelve states.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The opening clause of Article 5 states the collective defense principle and limits it to Europe and North America.
design.evidence_quote: an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America shall be considered an attack against them all

items.stem: Which of the following was most directly a later Soviet response to the alliance created by the treaty in the excerpt?

options.text: The creation of the Warsaw Pact after West Germany was admitted to the Western alliance in 1955
options.label: key
options.why: In May 1955 the Soviet Union formed the Warsaw Pact, a mutual defense alliance with its Eastern European satellites, right after West Germany joined NATO. This deepened the division of Europe into two blocs.

options.text: The launch of Sputnik, the first artificial satellite, which demonstrated Soviet advances in rocket technology in 1957
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Sputnik was part of the space and missile race, not an answer to the North Atlantic alliance as such.

options.text: The invasion of Czechoslovakia by Soviet-led forces to end the reform program of the Prague Spring in 1968
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The 1968 invasion was aimed at reform inside the Soviet bloc, not at the Western alliance.

options.text: The founding of Comecon to coordinate the economies of Eastern Europe as an alternative to the Marshall Plan
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Comecon was founded in January 1949, before the treaty was signed, and it answered the Marshall Plan rather than the alliance.

facts: West Germany joined NATO in May 1955.
The Soviet Union and its Eastern European allies formed the Warsaw Pact in May 1955.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The treaty's mutual defense pledge among Western states is the alliance that the Soviet bloc later answered with its own collective defense pact.
design.evidence_quote: shall be considered an attack against them all

items.stem: The collective defense provision of Article 5 in the excerpt was first formally invoked by the alliance in response to which of the following?

options.text: The terrorist attacks carried out against the United States on September 11, 2001
options.label: key
options.why: NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time after the September 11, 2001 attacks. A provision written to deter Soviet attack was applied to terrorism, which shows both continuity and change in the alliance.

options.text: Argentina's 1982 seizure of the Falkland Islands, a British territory in the South Atlantic
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: The Falklands War was real, but the islands lie outside Europe and North America, the area Article 5 covers, and the article was not invoked.

options.text: Russia's 2014 annexation of Crimea, which led eastern members to seek urgent consultations with allies
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Ukraine was not a member. The eastern allies' requests fall under Article 4 consultation, not an invocation of Article 5.

options.text: The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979, which ended détente and led to a Western boycott of the Moscow Olympics
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Afghanistan was not a member state, so Article 5 did not apply.

facts: NATO invoked Article 5 for the first time after the attacks of September 11, 2001.
Argentina occupied the Falkland Islands in 1982, leading to war with Britain.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article 5 defines an armed attack on a member in Europe or North America as an attack on all, and the attacks of 2001 on the United States were treated as such an attack.
design.evidence_quote: an armed attack against one or more of them in Europe or North America

items.stem: The excerpt's references to the United Nations Charter and the Security Council most directly reflect which postwar context?

options.text: The creation of the United Nations in 1945 as an organization to preserve international peace
options.label: key
options.why: The treaty grounds its defense pledge in Article 51 of the UN Charter and promises to report to the Security Council. Both belong to the international order set up in 1945 at the end of the Second World War.

options.text: The founding of the League of Nations after the First World War to settle disputes through arbitration
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The League was an organization of the interwar years, and the treaty refers to the United Nations, not the League.

options.text: The signing of the Helsinki Accords, in which Cold War rivals recognized postwar borders and human rights
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Helsinki Accords were signed in 1975, decades after the treaty.

options.text: The establishment of the European Coal and Steel Community to integrate the heavy industry of France and West Germany
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The ECSC was a 1951 economic organization and has nothing to do with the treaty's references to the UN.

facts: The United Nations was founded in 1945, and its Charter recognizes the right of individual and collective self-defense in Article 51.
The European Coal and Steel Community was created in 1951.

design.key_evidence_in_source: Article 5 cites Article 51 of the UN Charter and requires reporting to the Security Council, which ties the alliance to the UN system created in 1945.
design.evidence_quote: recognised by Article 51 of the Charter of the United Nations

items.stem: The provisions in the excerpt best explain which of the following developments in the Holy Roman Empire after 1648?

options.text: It limited the emperor's power over the princes, leaving the Empire politically decentralized.
options.label: key
options.why: The treaty confirmed the princes' territorial rights and their freedom to make alliances. That left the emperor with limited real authority over a loose collection of states.

options.text: It strengthened the emperor's power to direct the princes' foreign policy and so centralized the Empire.
options.label: reversal
options.why: This gets it backward. The excerpt gives the states their own right to make alliances, which weakens imperial control over foreign policy.

options.text: It ended the Empire as a political body by making each German state fully independent of the emperor.
options.label: overstated
options.why: The states stayed bound by their oath to the emperor and the Empire, and the Empire lasted until 1806.

options.text: It placed the German states under Prussian leadership, preparing the way for a unified German nation-state.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Germany was unified under Prussian leadership in 1871, more than two centuries later. The treaty itself kept the states divided.

facts: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) confirmed the territorial sovereignty of the German princes, including their right to make alliances.
The Holy Roman Empire continued as a decentralized body until its dissolution in 1806.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt confirms the princes' rights and 'free exercise of Territorial Right' and lets each state make alliances with foreign powers. Together these provisions limit the emperor's authority.
design.evidence_quote: free exercise of Territorial Right, as well Ecclesiastick, as Politick Lordships

items.stem: The treaty's promise that the imperial states 'never can or ought to be molested' in their rights was most likely a response to which of the following situations?

options.text: Wartime Habsburg efforts to impose imperial authority and Catholic policies on the princes
options.label: key
options.why: During the Thirty Years' War, Emperor Ferdinand II tried to expand imperial power and restore Catholic lands, for example through the Edict of Restitution of 1629. The princes wanted guarantees against this happening again.

options.text: Napoleon's reorganization of the German states into the Confederation of the Rhine under French protection
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Confederation of the Rhine was formed in 1806, long after 1648.

options.text: The conflict between Charles I and Parliament over taxation and royal prerogative in England
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: The English Civil War was happening at about the same time, but it was a separate English conflict and was not what the German treaty settled.

options.text: The Ottoman siege of Vienna, which threatened Habsburg lands and divided the German princes over defense
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Ottoman siege of Vienna took place in 1683, after the treaty.

facts: Emperor Ferdinand II issued the Edict of Restitution in 1629, ordering Protestants to return Church lands taken since 1552.
The Thirty Years' War (1618-1648) began with a revolt in Bohemia against Habsburg rule.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the treaty ended the Thirty Years' War, and the text's guarantee against being 'molested' on 'any manner of pretence' answers wartime imperial attempts to override the princes.
design.evidence_quote: they never can or ought to be molested therein by any whomsoever upon any manner of pretence

items.stem: The limits on imperial authority shown in the excerpt most directly contributed to which of the following developments in the century after 1648?

options.text: Habsburg rulers focused on building a power base in their hereditary lands, such as Austria and Bohemia.
options.label: key
options.why: With little real power over the Empire as a whole, the Austrian Habsburgs built up their strength in the lands they ruled directly, including Austria, Bohemia, and later Hungary.

options.text: Emperors in the 1700s created a unified imperial army and tax system that subordinated the princes to Vienna's control.
options.label: reversal
options.why: No such centralization took place. The Empire stayed fragmented, and the princes kept their own armies and finances.

options.text: The German princes formed the Zollverein customs union, which eliminated tariffs among most German states.
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Zollverein was created in 1834, which falls in the nineteenth century, not in the century after 1648.

options.text: The Pragmatic Sanction ensured that all German princes accepted Maria Theresa's succession without any war.
options.label: misattributed
options.why: Prussia rejected the settlement and invaded Silesia in 1740, which set off the War of the Austrian Succession.

facts: After 1648 the Austrian Habsburgs concentrated on their hereditary lands of Austria, Bohemia, and Hungary.
Frederick II of Prussia invaded Silesia in 1740, starting the War of the Austrian Succession.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The excerpt secures the princes' territorial rights against the emperor. This pushed Habsburg power-building into the lands the dynasty held directly.
design.evidence_quote: establish'd and confirm'd in their antient Rights, Prerogatives, Libertys, Privileges

items.stem: Which of the following best describes the excerpt's claim about the imperial states' relations with foreign powers?

options.text: Imperial states may ally with foreign powers if the alliances do not target the emperor or the Empire.
options.label: key
options.why: The text allows alliances 'with Strangers' as long as they are not 'against the Emperor, and the Empire.'

options.text: Imperial states are forbidden to make alliances with foreign powers so that the emperor controls all diplomacy.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The excerpt says it shall be 'free perpetually' for each state to make such alliances.

options.text: Imperial states may make foreign alliances only after receiving the emperor's formal approval for each agreement.
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The excerpt sets limits on what an alliance may do, but it never requires the emperor's approval.

options.text: Imperial states are released from their oath to the emperor whenever they join an alliance with a foreign power.
options.label: reversal
options.why: The text says alliances must be made 'without prejudice to the Oath' binding each state to the emperor.

facts: The Treaty of Osnabruck (1648) granted the imperial estates the right to conclude alliances with foreign powers, with limits.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The alliance clause grants the freedom and then limits it with the provision that alliances must not be against the emperor and the Empire.
design.evidence_quote: to make Alliances with Strangers for their Preservation and Safety; provided, nevertheless, such Alliances be not against the Emperor

items.stem: The treaty's guarantee of the German states' rights is best understood in the context of which broader development in European international relations after 1648?

options.text: Diplomacy that sought a balance of power among states to prevent any one dynasty from dominating Europe
options.label: key
options.why: Westphalia kept Germany divided and checked Habsburg ambitions. That fits the wider pattern of states balancing power against any one dominant dynasty, a pattern later seen in the coalitions against Louis XIV.

options.text: Renewed papal authority to arbitrate disputes among Catholic rulers and to approve the terms of peace treaties
options.label: reversal
options.why: Pope Innocent X condemned the settlement, and the peace was agreed without papal approval. It actually marked a decline in papal influence over diplomacy.

options.text: The confirmation of Spanish Habsburg supremacy over Europe through a permanent alliance with the Austrian branch
options.label: reversal
options.why: Habsburg power declined after 1648. Spain recognized Dutch independence in 1648 and lost ground to France in 1659.

options.text: The settlement of the Congress of Vienna, which restored legitimate monarchs after the defeat of Napoleonic France
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The Congress of Vienna met in 1814-1815, long after the Westphalian settlement.

facts: The Peace of Westphalia (1648) recognized the independence of the Dutch Republic and the Swiss Confederation.
Pope Innocent X protested against the Peace of Westphalia.

design.key_evidence_in_source: By guaranteeing that each state could make its own alliances 'for their Preservation and Safety,' the treaty helped create a system of many independent powers balancing one another.
design.evidence_quote: it shall be free perpetually to each of the States of the Empire, to make Alliances with Strangers

items.stem: The data in the table are most useful for studying which of the following nineteenth-century developments in Europe?

options.text: Population growth as death rates fell faster than birth rates
options.label: key
options.why: The table compares birth and death rates by region for two half-centuries. That makes it a direct measure of the nineteenth-century population growth that came mainly from falling mortality.

options.text: The Malthusian collapse of population caused by repeated famines across the continent
options.label: overstated
options.why: Europe's population grew a great deal between 1800 and 1900. There were local famines, such as Ireland's in the 1840s, but no continent-wide collapse.

options.text: The rapid rise of fertility caused by the abolition of serfdom throughout eastern Europe
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: Serfdom was abolished, for example in Russia in 1861, but historians do not explain European population growth as a fertility boom caused by emancipation. The table does not show that link either.

options.text: The decline of agricultural output after the enclosure of common lands
options.label: reversal
options.why: Enclosure and the agricultural revolution raised farm output. They did not lower it.

facts: Europe's population roughly doubled during the nineteenth century, from about 190 million to about 400 million (1800-1900).
Falling mortality was the main driver of nineteenth-century European population growth; birth rates fell later.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table gives birth and death rates per 1,000 for European regions in 1801-1850 and 1850-1900. These are the components of natural population growth.
design.evidence_quote: Birth and death rates in Europe by region, 1801-1850 and 1850-1900 (annual rate per 1,000 of population)

items.stem: Which comparison drawn from the table would best test the claim that European population growth in the nineteenth century came mainly from falling mortality?

options.text: Comparing changes in death rates with changes in birth rates between the two periods
options.label: key
options.why: Testing whether growth came from falling mortality rather than rising fertility requires comparing how death rates and birth rates changed from 1801-1850 to 1850-1900. The table supplies both.

options.text: Comparing the birth rates of different regions within the 1801-1850 period, without any later data
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Birth rates from one period alone cannot show change over time, and they say nothing about mortality.

options.text: Comparing the total populations of the largest European capital cities in the year 1900
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The table gives regional rates per 1,000, not city population totals. Totals for one year could not separate the effect of births from the effect of deaths.

options.text: Comparing the numbers of emigrants who left each region for the Americas after 1850
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Emigration figures are not in the table. They measure migration, not natural increase from births and deaths.

facts: Natural increase equals the birth rate minus the death rate.
In western and northern Europe, death rates declined across the nineteenth century, and sustained fertility decline began later in most countries (except France).

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table has birth-rate and death-rate columns for each of two periods. Students can therefore compare how each rate changed.
design.evidence_quote: Birth and death rates in Europe by region, 1801-1850 and 1850-1900

items.stem: Which of the following developments most directly contributed to declining death rates in western European cities in the second half of the nineteenth century?

options.text: Municipal sewers and clean water supplies, aided by the germ theory of disease
options.label: key
options.why: Public health reforms cut deaths from waterborne disease in the later 1800s. Examples are London's sewer system of the 1860s and Britain's Public Health Act of 1875, reinforced by the germ theory work of Pasteur and Koch.

options.text: The extension of the vote to working-class men in Britain by the Reform Acts of 1867 and 1884
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: These franchise reforms were real, but they were political changes. They were not a direct cause of lower mortality.

options.text: Mass emigration from Europe to the Americas, which removed millions of people from the continent
options.label: true_but_not_responsive
options.why: Emigration lowered population totals, but it did not lower the death rate per 1,000 of those who stayed.

options.text: The Romantic movement's celebration of nature and rural life
options.label: unrelated_development
options.why: Romanticism was a cultural movement. It had no direct effect on mortality.

facts: Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch established the germ theory of disease in the 1860s-1880s.
Britain passed a Public Health Act in 1875; London's main sewer system was built in the 1860s.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table covers death rates for 1850-1900, the period when urban sanitation and germ theory spread in western Europe.
design.evidence_quote: annual rate per 1,000 of population

items.stem: EXTRA. Which of the following is a limitation of the table for a historian studying mortality in Europe during the 1840s?

options.text: Half-century regional averages hide short-term crises such as the Irish famine
options.label: key
options.why: The table averages rates over fifty-year periods and broad regions. A sharp crisis like the Irish famine of 1845-1849 would be blurred into the 1801-1850 figures.

options.text: The table records only birth rates and omits any measure of deaths during the period
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The title states that the table gives both birth and death rates.

options.text: The table covers only the years after the revolutions of 1848 and omits the first half of the century
options.label: reversal
options.why: The table includes a 1801-1850 period as well as 1850-1900.

options.text: The figures reflect only British data because the source is a British encyclopaedia
options.label: unsupported_by_source
options.why: The context line says the estimates are by a Swedish statistician and cover regions of Europe, not only Britain.

facts: The Irish famine of 1845-1849 killed about one million people.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The table reports rates as averages for 1801-1850 and 1850-1900 by broad regions, so it cannot show crises of single years.
design.evidence_quote: it gives estimates by the Swedish statistician Gustav Sundbarg for regions of Europe

items.stem: EXTRA. Compiling estimates like those in the table depended chiefly on which nineteenth-century development?

options.text: Governments' regular censuses and civil registration of births and deaths
options.label: key
options.why: Nineteenth-century states built regular censuses and civil registration systems, for example Britain's census from 1801 and civil registration in England from 1837. These systems produced the counts that statisticians like Sundbarg needed.

options.text: The invention of the printing press, which allowed tables of figures to circulate widely
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: The printing press dates from the mid-fifteenth century. It did not produce nineteenth-century vital statistics.

options.text: Church parish registers newly introduced by the Council of Trent's reforms of the 1560s
options.label: wrong_period
options.why: Trent's registers date from the sixteenth century. Nineteenth-century estimates relied increasingly on state record-keeping.

options.text: The founding of the International Workingmen's Association to document labor conditions
options.label: misattributed
options.why: The First International (1864) was a socialist organization. It did not collect national birth and death statistics.

facts: Britain held its first national census in 1801.
Civil registration of births and deaths began in England and Wales in 1837.

design.key_evidence_in_source: The context line says the figures are a statistician's estimates for European regions. Such estimates rested on state census and registration data.
design.evidence_quote: it gives estimates by the Swedish statistician Gustav Sundbarg for regions of Europe
